Goldstein is obviously very erudite, and tries to wear her mantle of knowledge gracefully, but this book requires a reader with high tolerance for attenuated academic debate. Whether you happen to believe in god or not, this book will not enlighten you. The arguments pro & con are superficial and not very well presented. The "showdown" at the end of the book, featuring an academic debate about god's existence, is really simplistic & misses the most compelling arguments on both sides (the fact that it might be a good idea to have an objective criterion of morality in no way "proves" that such a criterion exists, any more than the fact that it might be nice to have a cure for cancer "proves" that such a cure exists. Conversely, a-theism, which is by definition an "absence of belief," does not require "proof" of why the person does NOT believe. The burden of proof is necessarily on the proponent of the belief. If I affirmatively assert that moon is made of green cheese, the burden is on me to prove that contention, not on you to DISprove it).  Apart from the dubious "theodicy," the book is a fun academic romp, with some well-drawn & interesting characters (Cass, Roz, Gideon) and other appalling ones (Klapper, Mandelbaum, Pascale), who may refresh your recollection of why you didn't finish your doctorate program.

An interesting plot twist is that both of the lead character Cass's (longer term) romantic partners are utterly vile people.  Despite supposedly being a brilliant psychologist, Cass somehow got hitched to a totally infantile, vague, selfish and not particularly bright French "poet" (Pascale) who seems to be a send-up of all things "French," and then fall head over heels in love with an AWFUL caricature of a totally self-absorbed narcissist (Mandelbaum) who can't be bothered to remember key events in Cass's life (that she herself pushed him into) and leaves him (!) when he has the audacity to get an offer for a better job than she has. She is utterly hideous, and it is baffling that anyone could fall in love with her, since she has filled that role to bursting, herself. I wonder (pure speculation) whether the author based this uniquely unpleasant character on one of her current husband (Steven Pinker's) ex-wives, the first of which is still an academic at Harvard.  I also found Goldstein's depiction of the boy genius mired in the rut of Hasidism genuinely tragic (in the Greek sense).  I wonder whether the heart-breaking absurdities in the lead characters' personal lives is part of Goldstein's point - of the limited nature and effect of rational approaches to the world at all.  If so, well-played.

review_text:
I am of two minds about this book, which, I think, is itself of two minds.  The book is definitely a history of America, 1860-1900.  But it tries to be two different books about that period. One is a generalist-level popular history with well-told stories about events that have made their way into popular culture like Custer's Last Stand, the 1871 Chicago fire, some Teddy Roosevelt stories and so forth, that have nothing or little to do with "capitalism".  The other is an economic history about the growth of big business and its conflict with populist sentiment.  Each one is fine by itself, but they didn't particularly cohere, to me.  Each one tends to dominate at different times (the economic story seems strongest at the beginning and end, for instance), but again, they don't really interweave.  Rather, it seems as if the popular stories are added to leaven the economic story. Or the economic angle was played up to tie it more closely to current concerns.

Occasional interjections of the author into the narrative make it seem as if ther is an integrating theme of "capitalism subverting democracy" but really I didn't feel the bulk of the book is about that.  The bulk of the book is basic late 19th century US history. The chapters on armed forces overcoming Native Americans, for instance, have nothing to do with capitalism.  To the extent that is the author's thesis, I felt he did a weak job of presenting it, and again, it felt a little strained.  At times, it seems as if he equates any method of making money as "capitalism" which is a superficial thought (e.g., think of nations like Russia, China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, where the major economic operations are controlled by oligarchies with close ties to government, often ties to the nation's military, who get rich by extracting rents from those operations and also from basic corruption, none of which can be argued to be "capitalism"). One anecdote in the book really brought this home to me.  At pages 395-97, the author recounts an episode in which a white grocer in Memphis came to feel threatened when some black citizens began a competing business. So he provoked an altercation with some of the black men, then complained to the local lawmen, who promptly arrested the black men, who wound up being lynched. That episode proves the opposite of "capitalism subverting democracy": it shows a member of an electoral majority using government power to destroy capitalistic business competition from an electoral minority.  Yet the author gives the impression this is another example of his theme, which just had me shaking my head in puzzlement. I will admit that when the author is focusing on obvious "capitalist versus worker" events, like strikes and farmers' plights, his theme comes through better.
But the "capitalism vs democracy" thesis failed to impress me.

The book is written at a general reader's level, and, for better or worse, contains hardly any quantitative analyses or presentations. (all the data documenting the many improvements in the economics of daily life during this period are jammed into two pages late in the book and followed by a "but..." of equal length). Even so, it's a pretty long read at 556 pages.  I think that is in part because it is, frankly, kind of choppy. Figures come and go, then reappear many chapters later. Chapters are grouped into broad thematic categories but there is no narrative continuity between them.  As a result of this approach, the kind of continuity that makes for a brisk, or even a cogent, read was not often present.

One thing I wondered about as I got deeper into the book was whether this was meant originally to be more of a general history of the period, but, in the wake of the 2008 financial crises, was tweaked to play up the "capitalism" theme, either at the publisher's behest to boost sales, or by the author because that was the way he was feeling about current events while editing it.

The plot is all about pregnancy and the different perspectives on it and babies. I did not enjoy the outcome of this one as it essentially involved Paige being forced into a situation she didn't particularly want or have a choice in. I felt like it was a violation of her agency and a happily ever after doesn't have to end in babies all the time.

review_text:
I wanted to read this book in hopes of helping me understand my introverted and sometimes shy daughter.  By the end of the book, I had a better insight into my whole family and most of the people I work with.  This book is a fascinating tour of the research on how different introverts and extroverts really are - and yet how they can work so well together.

What Cain has done here, and why this book is so well-written, is pull together a wonderful mixture of university research, interviews with dozens of people, and her own life experiences. I never felt like I was being bogged down in boring details of some 1,000+ page research paper or that this was simply some gathering of anecdotal evidence.  It is apparent that Cain did her research, laid out the work in a logical and easy to follow manner, and created a book that should be required reading in college sociology courses.

Usually I skip around in non-fiction books, but found myself reading every chapter of this one.

Fascinating reading - highly recommended.

Pat Buchanan's well written, thoroughly researched, fascinating look at what he calls "the unnecessary wars" of WWI &II was hard to put down. I've always thought very highly of Winston Churchill and was surprised to say the least that he wasn't the wise, truly concerned with England's and democracy's future leader that history has portrayed him as. While he was brave, heroic even as far as not caving into the enemy, he was hot headed, cruel, and had many other rotten leadership qualities. While the West won both world wars, several peaceful empires fell (the Hapsburg,the Romanov, the Prussian and the Ottoman at the end of WWI and England's after WWII), Eastern Europe ended up in the brutal hands of Stalin at the end of WWII, millions of people lost their lives as a result of these horrible wars, and so much more. As bad as Hitler was, Stalin was even worse in the number of people he tortured and killed. All of the Baltic and Scandinavian countries would have run into Hitler's arms, rather than be controlled by Stalin. I really appreciated the thorough research that allowed me to understand what really happened during that nasty time period. Also, even though I have never had anything except disgust for for FDR and his numerous Socialist programs the information on him was also most interesting and yes, rightfully in my opinion condemning.  One very surprising element detailed in the book was Hitler's love of England and the West and the fact that he didn't want to take them over and wasn't bent on world conquest as Stalin was. He had a much more limited goal. Even with his hatred of the Jews, the final solution for them wasn't devised until well into the war. Hitler hated the Bolsheviks every bit as much as the Jews and wanted to reclaim the Russian territory that Germany had taken in WWI and then was denied the right to control. Even though the book is long, the print is large and especially if like me you love history the book is engrossing. Even if you aren't a history buff, I highly recommend it. Because there is so much to say about this book, many of the reviews are long. So enough already. You'll have to read the book and find out the rest.

review_text:
Scott Sigler's, INFECTED, has been described as a must read, for Stephen King fans.  Well, I've always been a King fan, but have to admit I had to put 'CELL' down, without completing it, due to the bloody mayhem that just seemed like gratuitous violence, with little believability.  Not so, with INFECTED. From the moment I picked up this book, I hated to put it down, suffering serious sleep deprivation over the course of two nights---and this type of horror/thriller, with blood oozing off of every page is NOT typically my genre.  So, I'm quite confident in saying, that if it IS your type of read, you might want to call in sick and, devour it all in one day, for ultimate enjoyment. Be warned, you may be calling in sick the following day, too, as you hunt for your Pink Floyd t-shirt, with the triangle logo, because it's suddenly bothering you---and, you'll want to closely monitor those little chigger bites that, up until now, have only been mildly annoying. You'll probably want to put the kitchen utensils under lock-and-key, too,---just in case.

Yes, Sigler's creativity has taken the very familiar theme of alien invasion to a new level, when tiny alien seeds begin impregnating the skin of unsuspecting victims, turning them into psychotic, homicidal maniacs. As these little invaders develop, they begin to command the victims. Oh, and just wait until you read about the eyes. Eww! Their ultimate goal is not to be human, best-friend's-forever, either.

I thoroughly enjoyed the cast of characters: Perry Dawsey, the ex-football star, fighting off one of those demon seeds; Margaret Montoya, the CDC epidemiologist; and CIA agent Dew Phillips. The development of these characters was well drawn out, particularly with Dawsey.  His early life experiences, and disappointments, certainly set him up for being stoic and, taking-it-on-the-chin, until it was too late---or was it? The adrenaline pumping race was on to find out.

Be aware that this is an adult read, with grotesque violence, blood and gore, throughout. There is also quite a bit of profanity and general creepiness, that would not be fitting for young folks, or the faint of heart.  You must be the appropriate audience and prepare yourself for the, HORROR of INFECTED, before you can safely dive in. If you meet those requirements, fasten your seat-belts and enjoy the ride!

Alexander McCall Smith, the popular author of The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency, published a serialized column called "44 Scotland Street" for the Edinburgh Scotsman, which was turned into a book by the same name. It was a tongue-in-cheek peek at Edinburgh society, complete with returning characters whose lives intersect with a group of people who live at the fictional address in Edinburgh's New Town.

THE UNBEARABLE LIGHTNESS OF SCONES is the fifth book in this series, following on the heels of THE WORLD ACCORDING TO BERTIE, which featured the adventures of Bertie Pollock, a precocious six-year-old resident of the fictitious apartment building. Turning the spotlight on some of the other colorful characters is a delightful tale with a few more mysteries and insights into a growing cast of characters.

Bertie and his friends have decided to become Cub Scouts, which (he discovers to his dismay) must now legally accept girls. It was his one chance to escape the attentions of his schoolmate, Olive, who promises to grow up to be as insufferable as Bertie's mother.

Curmudgeonly Angus Lordie, a landscape and portrait painter, and his gold-toothed dog, Cyril, were left at the end of the last book with the product of Cyril's rendezvous in the park with an unnamed female of indeterminate breeding. Five months later, the mother dog's owner angrily rang the doorbell and deposited a box containing the six puppies on Angus's doorstep. Now Angus is left to figure out what to do with his population explosion. This story has not yet reached its denouement.

Sedate art dealer Matthew, newly wed and off with his bride on their honeymoon to Australia, discovers almost too late that adventure may not be a suitable lifestyle for him and his new bride. He also discovers a shocking skeleton in his family closet.

Domenica, Angus's close friend and confidante, is in an ongoing turmoil with an old friend and neighbor over a stolen Spode cup. Their tenuous relationship escalates to nearly insurmountable dimensions as suspicious deliveries begin to arrive at her door. There may also be romance in the air between Domenica and Angus, although two confirmed singles of a certain age might encounter unforeseen and quite possibly insurmountable obstacles.

Bruce, the vainest male in Scotland whose good looks have carried him far but never far enough, is confronted with reality in this installment. Can he become "The Face of Scotland," or will an epiphany of the heart save this narcissistic young fop from his foibles?

Big Lou, the owner of a local pub who has a reputation for bad taste in men, has her patience put to the ultimate test when her current boyfriend, a fervent Jacobite, brings the Pretender to the Throne of Scotland back from France to sleep on her couch until he can reclaim his title.

Gangster Lard O'Connor shows up unexpectedly at Matthew's gallery to have a potentially priceless (and no doubt ill-gained) portrait of poet Robert Burns appraised. This has Matthew, Domenica and Angus in a quandary as to how to handle it, especially when Lard drops dead at Lou's bar.

44 Scotland Street is almost a real address, but not quite. An examination via Google Maps shows the last address to be at Number 43. The people and stories in THE UNBEARABLE LIGHTNESS OF SCONES could also be true, according to McCall Smith in his Preface. He says that you can see these people any day in the New Town section of Edinburgh, which all lends a feeling of eavesdropping on the residents of this most Scottish city. One must wonder: Do the real denizens of Edinburgh glance covertly over their cocktail glasses at one another across a crowded party or a restaurant and think, I wonder if...?

  --- Reviewed by Roz Shea

In Oryx and Crake, we meet Jimmy (aka The Snowman), his friends the Crakers, and Oryx and Crake themselves.  In The Year of the Flood, we meet God's Gardeners and learn more about the waterless flood, a world-wide epidemic that wipes out nearly the entire human race.  In Maddaddam, Margaret Atwood completes her Maddaddam trilogy by bringing together the Crakers, the surviving God's Gardners, and the Maddaddamites, telling the story of their efforts to survive and preserve the human race, as radically different as it might turn out to be.

As the so-called waterless flood recedes, so to speak, these few survivors, whose lives have intersected extensively, come together to form a new community of sorts.  The humans, some of whom worked for Crake, unknowingly assisting as he planned the release of the global virus, mix and mingle with the children of Crake.  The Crakers, genetically engineered to be the next step in human evolution, and whose lives had been lived completely in an isolated biosphere, have had no contact with technology and human culture.  As they learn and adapt to human ways, the humans see that the survival of human life may depend on the thriving of the Crakers.

As with the first two books in this trilogy, the science is interesting, but frequently not very convincing, based more on fancy than science.  And the action of the story takes a back seat to the development of the characters and interactions of the groups.  The flashbacks, especially those of Zeb, whose brother Adam One founded God's Gardeners, shed more light on events before the waterless flood.

Readers of the first two books in this trilogy will likely be thrilled with Maddaddam.  I would recommend that you read Oryx and Crake and The Year of the Flood before you pick up Maddaddam.  The series as a whole is intriguing, somewhat though-provoking, and memorable.

A cogent account of our government's post-9/11 embrace of torture as an interrogation technique, this book's purpose is not to document the kinds of torture that have been applied (though there is some of that), but rather to trace the genesis of decisions and policies that led to it. The story of the past seven years is cast as a struggle between the rule of law and the belief that the president is the law (i.e., if the president does it/wants it/orders it, it can't be illegal). The result is a chilling picture of an administration sorely unprepared to govern in a time of crisis, unwilling to tolerate sound advice that runs counter to its assumptions, and a president utterly insulated from dissent and bad news.

While there is nothing new about the broad outlines of this account, Mayer manages to make the details gripping. The book is upsetting and enraging, but at the same time hard to put down--rather like watching a car crash.

Highly recommended.

This is a meticulously researched book, but what is truly impressive is Wilkie's gift for describing and understanding the people he depicts. Many readers will have heard of Scruggs and Mike Moore and Trent Lott, but almost none will know of the rural lawyers and backroom fixers who populate this book's moral universe. Yet Wilkie makes them all come alive, and makes you understand how vital they are to the story he is telling.

The comparisons to Grisham are inapt- Wilkie is writing at a much higher plane than Grisham.

If the book suffers from any obvious flaws, it is that Wilkie tends to parrot Scruggs's perspective in an uncritical fashion. No doubt, there were many professional jealousies at work. But before the corruption charges, Scruggs was repeatedly sued and excoriated for promising a share of his ventures to others and then not delivering. Efforts to illegally fix such disputes are what led to his imprisonment. Yet Wilkie tends to downplay these squabbles are mere money-grubbing efforts by the disappointed. He also portrays Scruggs's fall into corruption as an accidental one, not even initiated by Scruggs and joined only long after it was ongoing. Wilkie's attempt to tie everyone adverse to Scruggs--  but not Scruggs or his partisans- to the segregationist Senator Eastland, who had been gone from the scene for decades by the time the relevant events took place, also just seems made-up. It comes off as a convenient way of tarring Scruggs's opponents, perhaps unfairly.

One wishes Wilkie had been willing to connect the dots- when so many people, for so long, had contended that Scruggs ripped them off, perhaps the simple truth is that Scruggs was just rotten to the core. Wilkie doesn't go out of his way to acknowledge this possibility. Perhaps part of this comes from using many in the Scruggs camp as his sources. Perhaps too, there was a connection between himself and Scruggs- in the beginning, Wilkie describes seeing Scruggs at a dinner, and an exchange of personal notes prior to beginning the book.

However, all in all this book is fantastically written.

I know that I have used more than my fair share of bizarre metaphors, but how about this one; Douglas Preston and Lincoln Child are like peanut butter and chocolate; two great tastes that go great together. They have wrote some amazing books together, but on their own they are just as good.

The Forgotten Room is Lincoln Childs fourth suspense novel featuring the worlds only enigmalogist, Professor Jeremy Logan. Logan specializes in solving problems  that have unusual or even supernatural origins. In The Forgotten Room Logan is summoned to Lux, one of Americas oldest and most prestigious think-tanks, where he was once a member, to investigate the bizarre suicide of one of their most distinguished fellows. During his investigation into the Professors death, and the final project on which he was working, Logan discovers some disturbing clues, along with a ingeniously hidden secret room in an abandoned wing of the estate. Sealed off for decades, the room is full of mysterious equipment used for a top-secret experiment known only as Project S. Recruiting the Professors assistant, Kim Mykolos, and an architect, Kim Flood, whose firm worked on the building, Logan delves into this locked-room mystery.

All of Mr. Childs strengths are clearly on display in this work. He excels in giving us all of the details we need without slowing the pace or falling into endless exposition. All of the characters are fully realized, from Logan on down to people who only appear for a page or two. They all have interior lives, and all seem to have stories of their own. The prose is stripped, lean and mean, giving the reader what they need to know but never slowing the forward momentum of the narrative. I have an enormous amount of respect and admiration for writer who can write transparent prose. They may not get the kind of praise they critics heap upon people like Faulkner or Joyce,but in a book like this that skill is vital.

 The plot, like all of Mr. Childs, is full of twists and turns that genuinely surprise, but are in no way packed with tricks or gimmicks. Like all of Mr. Childs books, this books teems with research, and details; they say the Devil is in the details, but Mr. Child gives them to us in such a way that I could savor them even as I hurtled on through the pages, wanting to see how this story would end. That is probably the final test on which all thrillers are based, and The Forgotten Room does not disappoint. It is full of chills that are genuinely scary and made more so by their plausibility.

Tons of the plot I have to keep to myself, so that you can savor the surprises the way that I did,but it all works. The mixture of science and the supernatural, making the two shift and morph is one of the techniques that Mr. Childs utilizes wonderfully in this book, and I kept wanting to stop and research for myself if the things in this book were based on real events, but I could not, because I wanted to get to the end. At the same time I didn't want it end. When it does end, trust me, it ends with a big, big bang, in more ways than one. So bring on the next Jeremy Logan novel.

Having now read Jennifer Egan's award-winning and highly acclaimed novel, it is clear to me that this book and its author deserve every bit of praise heaped upon them thus far. The book introduces readers to Bennie Salazar, an aging and down-and-out music producer, and his assistant, Sasha, who experiences struggles of her own. Each chapter reveals parts of their past, told via the enthralling stories and lives of the many characters who enter and exit their lives.

What amazed me most about the book was how quickly I became totally engrossed in each separate (though not really!) character's short vignette. Egan creates a host of people that the reader comes to truly care about. The book is somewhat surprising and unique in its structure, as the author uses many different narrative forms to share each character's world, including second-person point of view narration, and even a slide presentation. Egan deftly intertwines the characters' distinct lives into one very readable work of modern fiction. I recommend this one to readers who enjoy literary fiction and 'character study'-type novels.

review_text:
What would happen if something mysterious and supernatural came to be in your possession? What if it was a book that had the ability to show you people's lives, including your own? Past, present, and future? What if you could see the doors open and close from the choices that were made and would be made? Would you be tempted to change the story? To make a different choice and walk through a new open door?

Mercy Land is a simple girl, but she has a "backbone full of worthy." She comes from the small community of Bittersweet creek, where her father is a traveling preacher, her mother is a God fearing woman, and her aunt has helped raise her with all the fiestiness she can muster. Mercy moves to Bay City, where she works for Doc Philips, an old man who runs the newspaper of Bay City. It is to Doc Philips that this book is entrusted to, and he soon calls on Mercy to help him find the reason why the book has been given to them. But Doc believes that he has found the reason the book has been given to him, and he believes it is his job to redeem Bay City from a choice that had been made a long time ago. A choice that affected someone from Mercy's past.

River Jordan is a wonderful storyteller. I liked that Mercy Land girl as soon as I met her, and Doc Philips is a man that I would like to meet some day. Mercy, a simple girl with a backbone full of worthy. And aren't we all, somehow simple? But full of worthy when we see ourselves for who God has made us to be? And wouldn't it be an honor if God entrusted us with something so precious because we have cared for others so deeply and made them feel important, just like Doc did throughout his life?

If you are looking for a great book to read, I highly recommend "The Miracle of Mercy Land."

There are at this moment 144 reviews for The Wave so instead of adding one more I am going to review the reviews.  My views of The Wave were expressed perfectly by K. Swanson (below).  The negative reviews were mostly based on one of four things: the book concentrated too much on surfing, the book concentrated too much on one surfer, namely, Laird Hamilton, the chapters on wave formation were not scientific enough, the author cites scientists who are concerned about the effects of global warming on waves and earthquakes and some people are so sure that global warming is a myth that they do not trust any book that says otherwise. Here are my recommendations: If you want a scientific treatise on the physics of waves buy a book by a scientist (good luck reading it).  If you have absolutely no interest in surfing or surfers, don't buy this book. If you are looking for a well balanced book on big wave surfing and  world class big wave surfers other than Laird, well, this ain't it.  If you want to keep your head in the sand (or wherever else makes you feel safe) about global warming, then avoid this book at all costs. I can recommend two books that better explain the science of waves from a pop science perspective. The first is Drew Kampion's The Book of Waves, which is a beautiful coffee table book that covers just about everything there is about wave formation from the first wind-generated ripples, to open-ocean wave trains, to the bathymetry that produces superior surf spots.  It is out of print but easily found in the used book market (some additions are very pricey).  The other book is Surf Science by Tony Butt which covers weather, climate, winds, currents, the Coriolis force, etc., etc., all geared toward understanding wave prediction for surfers.  As a surfer who has read dozens of books and hundreds of articles on surfing there was little in The Wave that I had not already read or seen in videos but I still enjoyed it very much.

But it's little more than a few relatively graphic sexual encounters combined with some of what I can only refer to as early 20th Century product placements.  The book drops so many names - mostly of luxury products but also some of the era's rich and famous people - that the confection becomes a bit too sweet and overwhelming.  The characters are completely cardboard cutouts and caricatures of themselves, and the notion that any musical composition in E-flat major will get a woman to surrender her virtue is, well, preposterous.

So while the book is pleasant enough, I really don't understand why all the fuss and rave reviews.

Without revealing spoilers, all I can say that this novel does not succeed as historical fiction, erotica, nor as a novel that creates characters about whom we care.  I was interested to learn of the abject materialism of the Burgher Dutch, as well as their evangelical Christianity, and also of the financial crisis of 1907, but the author failed to make the reader feel placed in that era, nor did he provide the reader with reasons to wish to turn the page to find out what happens next.  So little time, and so many other books I could have been reading.

review_text: I really enjoyed this book, especially the characters. London has dealt with her memory being wiped each night at 4:33 a.m. She leaves herself notes for the next day so that she knows what she wore the previous day, what she talked to people about, etc. I enjoyed reading London's story and felt for her not knowing the past but knowing the future. I cannot imagine knowing things about those that I love, especially knowing when they were going to die. I wish that we had learned more about her best friend Jamie but I am sure that it was good for London to know that through it all, she would always be there. I have to say that Luke was definitely swoonworthy and I did not see a few things coming in regards to his relationship with London. Their relationship was not rushed or pushed into something that they were not ready for and I enjoy books that deal with the main relationship this way. The ending was wrapped up nicely and I have heard that there will be no sequel so I am glad it ended that way. This book did make me cry in a few places when there were some surprising things revealed. I heard that this book has been optioned to be made into a movie and that Hailee Steinfeld has been chosen to play London. I finally just saw True Grit yesterday and I can really see her being a good London. I will definitely read more from Cat Patrick.

Like Rosamund Lupton's first novel, "Sister", her second book, "Afterwards", is written from the perspective of a female character bent on discovering the reasons and the people behind something bad that has happened to a loved one.  In this case, Grace looks to uncover how the fire in a school started and if it was directed at Jenny, her daughter.  As she investigates, Grace realizes Jenny is in danger, and struggles to keep her safe.  The main character in "Sister" directed her narrative towards her sister.  Grace directs her narrative towards her husband.

Lupton is good at creating women characters who face unusual obstacles in getting to the truth, and this is particularly true of "Afterwards".  During Grace's search for the cause of the school fire and the person or persons behind it, she discovers she has not always seen the people around her clearly and that she has taken, too lightly, things she should have noticed.  In this way, the novel is about revealing not only the mystery behind a fire, but also the mysteries and the secrets that the people Grace thinks she knows best have hidden from her.

Readers may be able to guess at least one of the characters behind at least some of the bad things in the book before Grace arrives at a solution, but it's the way Grace gets there that holds the readers' attention.

Although it is clear why Grace is so focused on Jenny, I did dislike the character a bit for giving short shrift to some of the other family and friends in the novel.  The "unusual" obstacles Grace faced seemed  little too much of a stretch at times, although the author's technique is interesting.

Four stars.

I read this book a long time ago and was so disgusted by the author that I promptly forgot about it until it crossed my path again recently and I re-read it. I went in with the intention of taking more time to look for the good points in the book, but despite my hopes, the entire documented experience struck me even more with the obviousness of child abuse by neglect. I'm not sure how a parent could think they loved their child and yet never exercise discipline for the good of that child. Two quotes popped out to me that I think explain Schofield's completely misguided philosophy better than anything I could say:

"But to be able to do what she can do at two years old, she must be a gift to humanity. I think that trumps being impolite on occasion."
and
"The imagination of kids her age seems to be limited to pretending to be princesses and crap like that. None of them are capable of conceiving of an entirely separate world like Janni is with Calalini."

Unfortunately, the complete arrogance of this father regarding his gifted and troubled child blinded him to the consideration that in order to function in society, manners are required even of geniuses, and that his daughter as he describes her early on in the book is not just impolite "on occasion" but totally out of control at all times. He also chooses to forget the fact that there are children out there even brighter than his own precious snowflake, and if one of them, raised in a normal home, met his precocious daughter, they might not even recognize her as a fellow gifted child because of her animal behavior. His permissive, excuse-making behavior was the main thing building a bubble around her throughout her early years, not her mental issues.

I write this as a child who grew up gifted, off-the-charts like Janni in verbal skills. I am not at all convinced that Janni's mental issues began as more than the extremely fertile imagination of any gifted child; I was also a world-builder who went far above and beyond the limited scope reported of Janni in the book, with made-up languages, cultural traits, geographical maps, even economic details. However, my parents knew to make sure I could delineate between real and imaginary, because after all, isn't that a sign of intelligence?  My creativity hasn't been stifled or curtailed by that realization in the slightest.

Throughout the book, all I could feel was pity for the many doctors, teachers, friends of the family, and random strangers who had to encounter Janni in her wild and untamed state. If Schofield was hoping to drum up understanding and sympathy with this book for his daughter, he failed utterly. I hope she has found peace and balance all these years later, but it's a shame that this obsessed father took so long to come to the realization that discipline walks hand-in-hand with loving parenting....to say nothing of the fact he practically urged her over the edge of imbalance and then sought powerful medication not meant for children which will have a profound negative effect on every cell in her body as she grows up. Other people have been bold enough to utter the phrase "Munchausen-by-proxy"...and I don't think it's an unreasonable accusation.
summary: Even more absurd on a second read-through.

review_text: The books were very well written. I found myself very emotionally attached to the characters. I loved how the books took you through growning into a woman.

Martha Beck was a doctoral student at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts with a husband and fellow doctoral student and a mother of a young daughter, Katie. In her second pregnancy, she learned that her unborn son had Down Syndrome. Nearly 75% percent of those diagnosed with Down Syndrome are terminated pregnancies. Martha was determined and her her husband to have their son and second child despite the cruel criticism by their peers, doctors, friends, relatives, and others of their decision to keep the baby.

In the end and even now, I don't believe there were any regrets about Adam. The nine months of the pregnancy can be a testament about marriages and relationships. Martha has no regrets about Adam's birth and life. The book begins with a trip to the psychic who claims Adam is an angel from heaven. This book is a terrific and easy read for those going through a similar situation. Martha writes candidly and honestly about her difficult pregnancy.

This book is not about a pro-life decision. As you know, the statistics are hard to swallow and read about having a Down Syndrome baby. Martha Beck and her husband made a decision to have Adam regardless of the test. They should be equally respected for that decision as well. They shouldn't be criticized or villainized for having Adam. So the book is a must read for anybody going through the same situation.

My grandfather was a master bombardier/navigator for the Air Force. During the Cold War, his mission was to be ready to drop nuclear ordinance on targets in the eastern USSR. The bombers did not have range for a round trip, so the orders were to ditch the plane and escape on foot through China.

In this book, we follow an air force pilot on just such a trek. It's a long journey, and it is a tale about the journey. It is an adventure story with a conclusion I found unsatisfying, but I'm glad to have followed Joe Mack on his travels. I saw Dr. Neal on the Today Show so I got this from the library to check it out first.  It started off all right with her childhood, but then it really lost me when she talked about her experiences in Mexico as Missionary when she was a teenager.

She claims that she accompanied these American missionaries who put her in charge of a maternity clinic where she performed and "supervised" deliveries and she claims, no kidding, that she performed C-sections.  How unbelievable is that?  Seriously?  There are medical doctors who don't have enough surgical skill to perform a C-Section so we're to believe that this untrained teenager did it?

After that she goes on about her kayacking trip to Chile and she gets trapped under water.  She talks about going into the light and meeting angels, etc., all good.  I'm still believing that part, but then she claims she kept going back to her body to please her rescuers and that explained why they noticed she kept gasping for air.

At this point I felt like she was trying to fit her story to the facts as those rescuing her saw them.  Then she claims she knew her son would die in the future.

I've experienced the loss of a child and I can tell you if I had foreknowledge that he would be killed in an accident, I'd do everything in my power to stop it.  She doesn't.  She doesn't really ever talk about life after death like you hear about in the accounts of children (Dr. Melvin Morse's books are the best) or in adult accounts.

This just isn't all that believable.  I do believe she had some kind of experience and that she did drown and come back to life, I just don't believe she had much of an "after life" experience.  And I certainly don't believe she ever performed a C-section when she was a teenager.

I'd recommend getting it at your local library first to judge for yourself and then buy the book if you are convinced.

review_text: This book is a heartfelt work, aimed to educate everyone interested in learning about near death experiences, what truly matters in life, and what may lie beyond for all of us. If you are interested in these topics, this is a highly recommended book for you. The author is Christian, but one of the things you learn is that religion does not matter, what matters as we move to the next plane of existence is love and compassion, not how you felt about religion during your time on this plane. This book is NOT political, and those who try to convince others that it is are incredibly misguided, lost and just sad. We as a nation in the US are suffering too much from negative spin put on the humane work of genuine people, with the lost ones trying to gain political points at the cost of human suffering. This negativity must stop, and will with the grace of God in all of us. It so happens that the politicians who reach out to the author's family on the sudden death of her oldest son are from one political party, but that's because he volunteered for that party. The nonsense about politics in some of the "reviews" on Amazon comes from a couple of sentences in the book, none of them promoting politics, but mentioning briefly how some truly honorable people who happen to be in politics reached out to offer sympathy to a grieving family, something that is certainly holy and above reproach! The boy was a skiier, and the skiing community reaches out too, that does not make it a book promoting skiing! If you are blinkered and narrowed in life so badly as to see what is not there, then that says so much more about you than about the book. Truly enlightened people look for the light in others, and don't keep guarding their personal hoard of darkness. There is so much to recommend about this book - the amazing description of the accident that almost killed the author, the incredible community response of prayer to help the author, a surgeon used to treating suffering in others suddenly going through suffering herself with grace and patience and an amazing capacity to learn. The true message of this book is to realize that there is more to us than our physical selves, more to learning than just memorizing, more to faith than clinging to the wreckage of ancient times, but in seeing the humanity in the wisdom of the ancients. Open your eyes and your soul will gain much from this amazing book. Highly recommended for all who are open to love and learning.
summary: Beautiful reminder of what matters in life and beyond - highly recommended for all

Before reading this book, I knew almost nothing about Tiffany lamps, other than what they looked like.  I always assumed they were created and designed by Tiffany.  I picked up this book because I heard that a woman named Clara Driscoll was behind the idea, creation and designs of Tiffany lamps and I wanted to learn more.  If you are looking for a good historical fiction read with a lot of detail on the creation of Tiffany lamps, you won't go wrong with Clara and Mr. Tiffany.  As a history and art history major in college, I found the story fascinating.

What I loved most about the book was the glimpse of New York City life at the turn of the century.  From walking the streets with Clara as she and her friends go to Times Square for New Years Eve, visiting the mansion of Louis Tiffany, walking the Lower East Side and viewing tenement living, riding the subway for the first time, bicycling around Lady's Mile to witnessing the creation of NY's first skyscraper, the Flatiron (a building I now work in), I felt like was there with Clara. I also loved learning about the process for creating the lamps.  I liked the amount of detail the author provided on the process of selecting the glass, creating the work, piecing it together, etc.

At first I was annoyed by Clara's "complaining" about never getting recognition for her work.  She did work for Louis Comfort Tiffany and rich customers were familiar with his name and therefore would be more willing to pay high prices for something designed by him, not by her.  But I had to step back and put her feelings/complaints in historical context.  I live in a time where women do get credit for their work and contributions.  When Clara worked for Mr. Tiffany, there were no equal rights for women, they couldn't join a union, they were dispensable and had absolutely no job protection.  Once I was able to understand where Clara was coming from, I appreciated her passion for her work and that of her Tiffany "girls."  Their craftsmanship deserved to recognized.

In reading other reviews, I've seen a few reviewers say that they would have preferred less detail on art and more detail on Clara's choice of art over love.  I disagree with them as I found her love life didn't add much to the story.  Yes, she had to chose her job over love (Mr. Tiffany wouldn't allow married women to work for him) a difficult decision for women in the early 20th century, but I felt at times that whenever the author introduced a new male character, Clara first thoughts always pertained to his potential as a mate.  Granted women did have to hitch their wagon to a man's since their opportunities were limited, I just felt that Clara was such an independent woman her focus on these potential partners detracted from the story.  But other than that, I had no major issues with the book.

Again, if you are looking for a good historical fiction read, pick this up.  You'll walk away with a great view of New York City and the woman behind the Tiffany lamps.
summary: a great glimpse into turn-of-the-century New York City

Lee Child's 15th Jack Reacher book is a milestone of sorts. A nominal sequel to 61 HOURS, which was published in May, it picks up shortly after the earlier novel. Reacher is a bit banged up as the result of his escape from what seemed to be a certain demise at the conclusion of 61 HOURS (in WORTH DYING FOR, he explains how he managed to remain intact), but his residual stiffness and limitations serve as a reminder that he is neither invincible nor invulnerable. He certainly possesses a skill set that makes it difficult to remember that he might have a few weaknesses. Nonetheless, Reacher retains enough to triumph against overwhelming odds here, utilizing his considerable mental and physical abilities to right some extremely horrific wrongs.

WORTH DYING FOR finds Reacher dropped off in the middle of a nowhere called Nebraska, with little around him but a deserted motel. A series of events puts him crossways with the Duncan family, who for a couple of generations have run the local farming community as their own little fiefdom, utilizing a combination of terror and economics. They handle all the trucking of the surrounding farmers' goods to market, and no one dares to use an alternative transport system. As far as they're concerned, it's either their way or the highway. The Duncans also traffic in other goods, and Reacher's arrival is both the fly in the ointment of their latest shipment and a convenient excuse when the delivery to their customers in the south is unexpectedly delayed.

Reacher soon finds himself to be the target of some very big and dangerous people, including the Duncans' de facto security force, which consists of some alumni of the Nebraska Cornhuskers football team, and enforcers representing different links in the sales chain, of which the Duncans are merely the first step. Reacher has few places to hide; his area has a whole lot of nothing, and the Duncans have most of the folks around there too terrified to help him. There are a couple of exceptions, however, including a woman victimized in the worst way by the Duncans several years before. Reacher would be just as happy to move on to where he was heading to begin with --- Virginia, for a rendezvous that may or may not happen --- but winds up staying, in part because of a mysterious tragedy that screams for resolution.

And thus we come to the strongest parts of the book. Reacher's combat skills consistently offer triumphs against his adversaries, but it's the mystery --- and Reacher's resolution of it --- at the core of these novels that makes the series worth reading. Here this process proceeds along two tracks --- one in which Reacher slowly unravels a horrific series of events in the Nebraskan cornfields, the other in which he takes the forces rallied against him and points them at each other. The result may or may not be the best Reacher book to date, but it certainly is his most satisfying.

I'm not sure what Lee Child has against the Nebraska Cornhuskers --- that his choice for a group of strong-backed and weak-minded associates would be best served by, say, alumni of the University of Michigan --- but regardless of your football loyalties, you'll find WORTH DYING FOR worth reading far into the night.

--- Reviewed by Joe Hartlaub

This is really a solid 3.5 star for me.  But since it is the most entertaining John Grisham novel I've read in years, I decided to bump it up to 4 stars rather than bump it down to 3 stars.

Oscar Finley and Wally Figg are the only 2 partners of a two-bit law firm in Chicago who specialize in quickie divorces, DUIs, personal injury, and an assortment of other cases that are basically the bottom-dwellers of the law profession.  Oscar, a sixty-something grouch trapped in an unhappy marriage, spends most of his time counting the days until he can retire; while Wally, a forty-something recovering alcoholic, is forever coming up with schemes that he says will make them millionaires.  Then, one day, one of Wally's clients tells him about this drug that is supposedly causing people to die of heart-attacks; and suddenly, Wally's dream of riches and corporate jets does not seem so far-fetched anymore.  Armed with nothing but the testimony of a half dozen unreliable witnesses and a couple of pages of research done on the internet, Wally files suit against one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in America; and thus begins the hilarious story of 3 men's attempt to milk the justice system for a quick buck.  Joining Oscar and Wally on this misconceived quest is David Zinc, a 31-year-old Harvard-educated lawyer already burnt-out by the daily grind of pushing papers for a large law firm.  And when the pharmaceutical company choose to not settle like the lawyers of Finley & Figg expect them to, our erstwhile "heroes" has no choice but to go to court and fight till the end, nevermind that none of them knows the first thing about trial litigation.

This is definitely not your typical John Grisham thriller. Instead of a hero who's fighting to right a grave injustice, you've got two sleaze-ball lawyers out to make a quick buck.  The author was careful never to take anything too seriously, so the result is a funny book that manages to gently mock the litigious society we've become without crossing the line into being sanctimonious.  Both Wally and Oscar are amoral but essentially harmless, so I found myself laughing out loud at many of their antics and their bumbling attempts to convince the judge, and plaintiff, and the cutthroat attorneys the plaintiff has hired that they actually have a case.  Interspersed with the shenanigans in the courtroom are the equally hilarious hanky-pankies that go on in their personal lives, which added an additional layer of comedy to an already vastly entertaining book.

What kept this from being a 5 star or even a solid 4 star book for me is the predictability of the ending.  The absence of a hero that you can root for also detracted from the enjoyment somewhat, although David Zinc did his best to be a straight-man's foil to Wally and Oscar's inept villainy.  Still, I enjoyed this book tremendously and would recommend it to anyone who's got hankering for a legal thriller with a heavy dose of the absurd.
summary: The most entertaining John Grisham novel I've read in years

Easy Rawlins is an easy guy to follow as he drifts through the underside of Los Angeles, looking for his quarry. The quarry is not always a bad guy, because almost everyone is a little bit bad in these novels, but whomever his client wants him to find. He has a checkered past, having grown up "in a hard place" which lends a certain outlook to his character. Unfortunately he has a character fault that ruins the positive aspects of these books. He simmers with a racial hatred that permeates his thoughts and his actions. He tries to do the right thing in most circumstances, except when he is angry, or under the influence. He is not above a fantasy about killing a white liquor store owner who reminds him of Grouch Marx, revealing the racism and anti Semitism that seems to come not just from Easy, but directly from the author.  Misunderstanding, fear, and rage against another because of their race is an evil force in anyone's heart, and Easy has plenty of evil forces surging through him.

Aside from that, Easy is presented as a good guy, who tries to do the right thing, sticks up for victims, and rescues those who need rescue. This story moves along at a relaxed pace. It is not a page turner, but it did hold my interest. The plot and the dialogue, the description and the characterization are all skillfully done. Easy makes occasional comments that reveal an active intelligence and a wide ranging intellect. The story is more thoughtful than most mysteries, and more interesting.

Mosley is a skillful and gifted writer. I was hooked by the first paragraph. Normally you don't expect good writing in a mystery, particularly a hardboiled detective story like those in the Easy Rawlins series. But Mosley has a way of writing beautifully and brutally in the same sentence. He speaks with an authentic voice, and speaks it well. All the problems and pathos of the urban desert that makes such a large part of 20th century America comes to a boil in these novels. It is a shame that some of those problems damage an otherwise excellent novel.

review_text: It is not easy for me to write a review of Destiny of the Republic that doesn't cover much of the ground that has already been noted in the 127 reviews previously posted. So let me contribute what little I can and avoid being repetitive. I've been an admirer of Garfield since 2003 when I read Ken Ackerman's DARK HORSE: The Surprise Election and Political Murder of President James A. Garfield. As you'd guess from my review (http://www.amazon.com/review/RC7CH7SFD5ZIF/ref=cm_srch_res_rtr_alt_1), it would take a pretty outstanding volume for me to consider it of equal quality. I feel that Candice Millard has fully succeeded in doing so. Up front, let me note this: I wouldn't have thought it possible to write a book that is in large part a biography of James Garfield without mentioning his pivotal role in the Battle of Chickamauga. But this book is much more than the phenomenal story of Garfield's life. Into the book are woven stories and intersections with Garfield's life of eight (perhaps more) significant individuals. Ms. Millard includes extensive information about the assassin, Charles Guiteau. If you didn't think him insane before now, you'll have no doubt of it after reading just a little about him. Alexander Graham Bell probably receives the next largest amount of coverage regarding his feverish efforts to refine a metal detector (induction balance) to pinpoint the location of the lead bullet lodged inside Garfield. Others who are covered with detail include Garfield's wife, Lucretia; US Senator Roscoe Conkling, who Garfield out-maneuvers and basically forces out of politics; Conkling's arch enemy and Garfield's Secretary of State, James G. Blaine; Garfield's running mate, Vice President, and successor, Chester A. Arthur; Joseph Stanley-Brown, who at just 22 years of age became the private secretary to President Garfield; and lastly, Joseph Lister and his development of antiseptic surgery, the practices of which were ignored and shunned by the treating physicians, led by D. Willard Bliss. The Epilogue concludes with a profound tribute to Lister by the US Ambassador to the Court of St James: " ... it is not a profession, it is not a nation, it is humanity itself which, with uncovered head, salutes you." How does "Destiny" differ from "Dark Horse"? This book is much more focused on telling you about the key players with interesting and not widely known events in their lives. Here are several examples: - You'll learn that Garfield was singing to his sons a song from Gilbert and Sullivan's H.M.S. Pinafore (I Mixed Those Children Up) the morning that he was shot by Guiteau. - She tells how Bell's efforts to fine-tune his metal detector were cut short when his wife, Mabel, gave birth prematurely and the infant died. - She provides insight into Chester Arthur and how he underwent transformation from a Stalwart, machine politician to a supporter of Civil Service Reform who signed the Pendleton Civil Service Act into law. It is through advice given him by Julia Sand, a young, invalid woman living in New York City with whom he corresponded at great length. Dark Horse has much more emphasis on the political events surrounding the era of Garfield's rise to prominence. It begins with "The Feud" in April 1866 between James Blaine and Roscoe Conkling that lead to their profound hatred of each other. The thread of this feud as it cascades through events for years to come is present throughout the book--fascinating history. There is much detail about the Republican Convention of 1880, including state-by-state tallies of the crucial ballots leading up to Garfield's astonishing nomination. There is also great insight into the tied US Senate in 1881 and how Vice President Arthur navigated through unchartered waters and used his tie-breaking vote as Senate President to give the Republicans control of the upper house. Both books are focused on the same event: the assassination of President Garfield. But the authors approach the event from different perspectives and each have produced superb tales of this tragic event and all the circumstances surrounding it. Along with the majority of the reviewers, I recommend the book as strongly as I can. It is a page-turner, beautifully written with an eye for detail, full appreciation of the setting of the events in our history, and I feel, a balanced view of the forces and personalities at play in the evolving events. Though you know Garfield is doomed, Ms. Millard weaves in key developments that keep your attention and admiration of this superb work.
summary: Great Companion to Ackerman's Dark Horse

Simply put, Shani Boianjiu is, as she proves in her debut novel, The People of Forever Are Not Afraid, one hell of a writer.  What makes the book especially remarkable is that Boianjiu is still not much older than the three young women whose coming-of-age stories are at the heart of her story.  In 2011, in fact, Boianjiu, at age twenty-four, became the youngest ever National Book Foundation "5 Under 35" honoree.

Avishag, Yael, and Leah are three high school girls living in a small Northern Galilee town where everyone, almost by necessity, knows everyone else.  The students, like young people in any small town, are generally bored with their lives and dreaming of life after high school.  The big difference for them is, of course, that as they turn 18 and leave high school, each student, male or female, will be required to serve two years in the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF).

The girls, when their time to enlist comes, enter the IDF at different times and have very different experiences.  Avishag becomes a guard responsible for keeping refugees on their side of barbed-wire fencing, Yael spends her days turning recruits into marksmen, and Leah becomes a checkpoint guard where she must be on constant alert for would-be suicide bombers.  Typically, the girls will spend more time fighting boredom than directly confronting the dangers of terrorism, but each will be aged (if not necessarily matured) and otherwise changed by their two years of military service.

Boianjiu allows her three central characters a first person voice to tell their own stories - but, because the voices are not always distinct, this can leave the reader unsure which of the girls is doing the speaking.  Using a series of flashbacks and back stories, she intertwines the three lives over a number of years as the young women struggle to maintain the friendships that were strained even before they left home for the military.

The People of Forever Are Not Afraid was originally conceived and published in short story format.  The incident in which three protesters request that border guards meet them with escalating levels of resistance (perhaps my favorite story in the book) is, in fact, one I remember reading in The New Yorker magazine some time back.  That the book was originally written as a series of standalone stories is both a strong point and a weak point.  On the one hand, the incidents, taken separately, are enlightening looks inside the Israeli military structure from a female point-of-view.  On the other, the narrative structure and what are often indistinct first-person voices make the "whole story" a rather difficult one to follow.

That said, it is obvious that Shani Boianjiu is a talented writer, and I look forward to a more conventionally structured novel from her next time out.  She has a bright future.
summary: Coming of Age in the IDF

If it seems like the last several elections hit us with unusual urgency, with an unprecedented number of earth-shattering issues and bold proposals, you're right. Not that life has become more fraught with peril and possibility (we could argue that), but the people who would become America's leaders have grown more savvy in pursuing their goals. Journalist Sasha Issenberg unpacks several recent developments in the science of American elections.

For years, candidates and their handlers have run campaigns as largely intuitive enterprises. Office seekers took sweeping patterns of behavior for granted, assuming that, for instance, flyers and TV ads got the message out. They also assumed voters were rational actors, voting their own interests, and that they voted basically on the belief that their single votes could swing the election. These assumptions had no scientific basis; electioneers just took them for granted.

Nobody thought to test such assumptions with laboratory rigor until the 1920s, when Harold Gosnell subjected different voter groups to targeted messaging. This was just after his home base of Chicago had instituted primary voting, letting candidates get on the ballot without the patronage of monolithic party machines. His discoveries, particularly about why free citizens don't vote, were published, heralded, widely read... and quickly forgotten.

After Gosnell, the science of political movement proceeded only by fits and starts. Despite its name, "Political Science" has largely been more a branch of philosophy than an actual science. Isolated discoveries during the middle of the Twentieth Century made for momentary leaps forward, and elections became a somewhat more refined enterprise. But politics remained the domain of professional chin-pullers who largely only talked to one another.

This in part stemmed from the risks inherent in serious testing. For a long time, the only way to see whether a particular message worked, was to set up a control group of voters who would not receive key messages. No candidate, obviously, wanted to give up key votes, particularly in closely contested elections, which were the ones that would yield the most meaningful results. So political science inched forward, relying on untestable beliefs.

Throughout the Twentieth Century, we could rely on certain constants: Democrats had better luck mustering volunteers to get out the vote. Republicans could curry more and bigger monetary donations to pay for media blitzes. To use the military metaphors beloved of campaign professionals, the Repubs had better air cover, while Dems did better at close quarter combat. But after the 2000 elections, everything began to change.

Real advances in understanding voting and campaigning came, not from within the political science fortress, but in economics. The rise of behavioral economics allowed a field previously famous for starched shirts and inscrutability to study why ordinary people do ordinary things. They discovered, for instance, that voters do not vote because we think we can swing the election; we vote because of social implications. We vote when others expect us to vote.

You remember what happened in 2000, right? You remember the Presidential election decided not by voters, but by a quirk of the court system. Republicans wanted to ensure their win wasn't seen as a mere quasi-legal fluke. Democrats wanted to restore what they perceived as diminished legitimacy to the electoral system. And behavioral economists were perfectly positioned to fill the need coming from both sides.

It would be easy for Issenberg to make this book about only one party. Dubya's ability to do the impossible and solidify his slippery grip in 2002 would have made an exciting story in its own right. So would Barack Obama's unprecedented ability to drum up small donors and sweep the election in 2008. But neither of these would have told the whole scope of the story, which Issenberg admits is far from done. New discoveries come out every day.

I feel a bit disappointed by Issenberg's approach. He promises "the secret science of winning campaigns," but focuses more on personalities than processes. Knowing who made important discoveries matters, and the range of personalities creates a narrative flow that binds the book together. But apart from a few discoveries (bullying, sadly works; front door visits from volunteers turn out more voters), he doesn't give us very many working points.

Still, Issenberg does give a good overview of recent developments, and his thorough source notes suggest further reading. He also reveals important avenues of investigation still open for boots-on-the-ground research. For anyone interested in politics, either as a voter or an activist, Issenberg shares ongoing insights and important open questions.

In the city of love and romance anything is possible. For three French tutors their world's are each turned on end by three very different American students. With nothing to lose after the death of her lover, Josie sets off for Paris on the trip that may change everything. For Riley, Paris is not a city of love but perhaps the place where she lost her love and passion for life until she meets Phillippe. Jeremy is lost for words when he meets his tutor Chantal. Each experiences something completely unique, but so similar; a discovery of who they are.

French Lessons was a completely unexpected read. When I initially picked it up I was at a book conference and fell in love with the cover (a different one than above). It was so much more than a simple book about two people meeting and falling in love. The novel was actually broken up into five sections: the opening, three sections with each tutor/student pairing and then the closing. What was wonderful about that aspect was that it made it easy to read a section at a time and savor that portion. Though, what I found impressive was that in each small section there was a story that drew me in and didn't let go until the last page.

It's difficult to say I had a favorite pairing or section of French Lessons, but if I had to I'd choose Josie & Nico with a close second to Riley & Phillippe. My only hesitation with Riley & Phillippe was the rather graphic sex scene, just not my thing, but otherwise I loved their story. With Josie & Nico though there was so much depth and character development that I've found myself wondering about where they might be now after I've already completed the book. Josie's character really got under my skin and though I'd normally dislike her because of her having had an affair with a married man, her grief at his death completely drew me in. It's hard to describe, but each of these characters were so well written that I couldn't help but be interested in who they truly were.

Readers looking for an incredibly well written character driven novel about love and discovery, than French Lessons is absolutely a book to pick up! Ellen Sussman's writing brings to life characters that may normally seem bland & predictable from the outside and instead makes them deep & charismatic. This is a story about three sets of very different people coming together to discover who exactly it is they each are and what they want from their lives. French Lessons is an absolute must read!

Walking with Jack

In a nutshell, this is a story that centers around a fathers journey to become a caddy for his son once he goes on the pro tour and concludes with an epiphany for both. If you don't like golf, this book isn't for you. I know a lot of the reviews say it is really about a father and son relationship, but if you absolutely do not care for golf then the book isn't for you. Much of the action and plot development centers around golf. I enjoy golf and found some of the discussions about the courses to be insightful and got me searching for them online to at least look at the course layout. However, Snyders play-by-play reports of several golf matches were interesting at first but got annoying to the point I skipped them just to find out what happens with him and his son.

I noticed a slight anti-war sentiment from the author in many parts of the book, but he reminds the reader that he had been working on a sports scholarship in order to afford to attend college or risk facing the draft to fight in Vietnam. This is certainly a hard decision to make, and I have to respect the authors constant choice of a strong work ethic to achieve his goals. Much of this attitude can be found in his son Jack. It was disheartening to read about Snyders experience with his boss at Colgate University, because it reminded me of many tenured professors and how they wield an enormous amount of power in the classroom.

Snyder also criticized Tiger Woods in many instances, mainly about how he treated his family with the various scandals. I felt this just conveyed Snyders strong concept of family and his work ethic. The first part of the book could be described as Snyders journey as a caddy in Scotland, while the rest of the book gives more insight into the pro tour and how failures aren't really shown on the Golf Channel but instead they tend to highlight the successes.

Overall: 4/5 stars, if you're not into golf then you may not like this book. Yes it does focus on a fathers relationship with his son, but it centers around their love for golf.
summary: A great golf story about a father, his son, and their love of golf

Goodbye For Now is mainly set in Seattle, Washington but setting isn't Ms. Frankel's main focus. She rarely gives detailed descriptions of the characters' surroundings. Only in the later chapters her writing becomes more pictorial and when it does, many things are left to the reader's imagination. Either that, or the author expects the reader to know about the geography of Seattle. But I didn't mind, because setting isn't that important in this novel. The characters and the story are what make it worth reading.

The three main characters are Sam, Meredith and Dash. The reader sees almost everything through Sam's eyes. He is a very likable character with a great sense of humor and is therefore easy to identify with. Meredith is a stereotypical woman. At first, she is very nice but later in the book she gets demanding and whiny. To make it short: She doesn't know what she wants and she really got on my nerves. Dash completes the trio by being very positive and social. He is a funny guy without wanting to be funny. Dash is a wonderful addition to the book as he helps to lighten up the darker parts. In my opinion, this trio of main characters is very balanced. Sam, Meredith and Dash are surrounded by various other characters, each with their own little story to tell.

The plot of Goodbye For Now is new to me. I like that Ms. Frankel introduces the pros and cons of a computer program that enables people to communicate with the "dead". She shows that this is not something that everyone would think of as good and she also points out that serious problems can arise. Goodbye For Now combines an easy to read writing style with a serious topic. This is not your usual love story. (Even if the German title suggests it) Goodbye For Now is a book that will make you laugh, cry and think.

A Clash of Kings is the second in the ongoing Song of Ice and Fire series, sequel to A Game of Thrones, and the series continues to be entertaining and interesting, one of my favorite ongoing fantasy series.  What makes it different from other fantasy series is that Martin, instead of using chapter numbers and having everything be specifically chronological, has about five to ten characters whose heads you are in.  So you can be immediately whisked away to another battle, another land, another family feud, by the turn of the page.  Plus Martin isn't afraid of killing off characters, which can be horrible if one gets really attached to certain characters, but I find it admirable that he has the bravery to do this.  I think it isn't done enough in fiction, specifically fantasy.  Sure the good guys need to win, but not all the time!

Near the end of A Clash of Kings there is huge battle between two big armies: one attacking the other on a river, beginning as a naval battle, and then once the men land on the ground, moving on to try breaking into the fortress.  Your regular historical or fantasy novel would have you in the head of your main character who would likely be one of the leaders of the armies.  The P.O.V. might switch during the battle to the other leader's viewpoint on the other side and then come back to your main character.  With Martin's literary device, the reader sees the battle unfolding from three interesting viewpoints: from the leader of the army in the fortress (who is an ugly dwarf); from one of the captains of the ships, on the other side, attacking the fortress, as he leads in the ship and engages the enemy; and from a young girl who is a hostage in the fortress, under the watchful eye of the queen, in a room full of the important women who are just waiting around to find out if they are on the winning side, or if they are on the losing side and the enemy is about to break down the door and the knight will be ordered to kill them all so they won't end up as hostages.  So instead of seeing the entire battle from one of possibly two P.O.V.s, the reader gets three totally different viewpoints, and it just heightens the tension and suspense.

Next in the series is A Storm of Swords, with A Feast For Crows due out November 8th, 2005.  As Martin was writing A Feast For Crows, passing the thousand-page mark a couple of months before the book was done, he was told by his publisher that they can't have one book be this long.  He'd previously promised that his next book would not be as long as A Storm of Swords, which was 1216 pages in the mass market edition.  Since he's going to long pass this, he negotiated with Random House to split the book in two.  What he's decided to do, and as I get further into the series I can't understand how he's going to do this, is have half of the characters in one book, and the other half in the next book.  Some of the characters can be on their own tangents, meeting different people, and not actually have anything to do with the other main character's whose heads the reader is in, but there are other characters who interact with each other quite often, and I just don't know how Martin is going to reconcile this.

It's going to be interesting, that's for sure.  And the good thing Martin said is that the new book comes out soon, and the next one is already half done.

Lee Strobel, once an atheist and now a committed Christian, is a master at these books.  I had already read "The Case for Christ" by Strobel and found it an excellent intellectual and pastoral approach to belief in Christ.  When I saw Strobel had written a book on faith, I thought I'd try this one as well. Again, an excellent approach to the question of faith.

Strobel is a master story-teller.  Each of the eight "objections" to faith which Strobel investigates (in chapter format) is introduced by an engaging story and anchored with an interview with a person known for writing/lecturing on that topic.  Through these devices, Strobel (mostly) holds the reader's attention.  (Some topics are obviously going to interest the reader more than others.)

These are tough objections to Christianity: suffering, miracles, evolution, God killing innocent children, Jesus is the only way to God, God tortures people in hell, Christianity is filled with oppression and violence, doubt and Christianity. I think that investigative reporter Strobel finds satisfying answers to the objections.

This is a book written by an Evangelical interviewing many Evangelicals; thus, the approach is different in some places than it would be for a Catholic like me.  But it was helpful to learn from other approaches.  I didn't read the book because of my own faith-questions, but because I wanted to see how articulate people answer these difficult questions.  I learned much and I think that the book helped me to understand some of these issues better, making me a better advocate of the Christian message, which I have come to embrace as life-giving Truth.  I appreciate anything that can help me to share and reflect that Truth to others.

I agree with Strobel that in the end, you have to take what you have and move with it.  You can try to get it clear in your head, which is helpful, but living it helps bring clarity and the knowledge that this is Truth.  That certainly helps make life worth living and much easier to talk with people struggling with faith issues.

I highly recommend this book.  My challenge now is that I have two more of Strobel's books to read!
