Nick Turse was a graduate student over 10 years ago when he was searching through the National Archives in Washington D.C. for information on his Ph. D. dissertation.  He had decided to do PTSD in Vietnam Veterans and was looking for information on the war.  A librarian asked if war crimes could be a reason for PTSD and gave him a bunch of recently unclassified documents about Vietnam War crimes that American troops committed.  No one was arrested, tried or charged in these crimes and while the report was well researched and documented, asking questions of soldiers, commanders, officers and Vietnamese civilians, they report was never released but left on a shelf to yellow.  When Turse copied a few documents and showed them to his dissertation mentor, David Rosner, who read the documents and told him to pursue the war crimes information as his dissertation instead.  David recommended that he copy all the documents as soon as possible and as quickly as he could.  When Nick said he didn't have the funds, David gave him the funds.  Nick spent several days copying the documents in the report from opening until closing.  It was a good thing, because soon after Nick wrote a news article about the documents, the documents were pulled from the public section of the Archives and reclassified as secret.  The report was began after the My Lai Massacre to discover how common massacres were in Vietnam by American troops and to make sure they never happened again.  The initial complaint that began the investigation was a soldier named Charles McDuff who witnessed several massacres and attempted to complain several times.  He was threatened by local soldiers and commanders and finally wrote a letter to President Nixon who sent the complaint to the Dept. of Defense but replied that he hoped that he had told his commanding officer in a way that seemed not to take him seriously.  Unbeknownst to him, the Defense Dept. did an investigation and corroborated what Henry said and then shelved the report.  The report found that from the presidency on down, there was an idea to kill as many Vietnamese as possible and that there would be no discrimination between enemy combatants and civilians.  Kill Anything That Moves was a common order from commanders.  This book details how the massacres became standard operating procedure for the war and the belief system behind it.  The government seems to have believed that running war like a corporation with debts and credits (as in bodies) would convince the Vietnamese of American invincibility and surrender.  An amazing book that just blew my mind.  It also makes me think of how the wars since have really been about testing new products (weapons) and that the US still doesn't seem to care about others' rights and territory.

Witherwood Reform School is the first book in a new series from Potterwookie author, Obert Skye. Like his other books, Witherwood is funny and often absurd. This offering is particularly reminiscent of Lemony Snicket's Series of Unfortunate Events. Like that series, Witherwood features siblings, dark humor, and some rather unfortunate luck.

One of my favorite things about this book was the narrator, who often speaks to the reader and comments on what is happening to the main characters, Tobias and Charlotte. Some books are well served by this kind of narration that breaks the wall between story and real life - I think this is a good example. There is a very distinct impression that, if the reader doesn't mind their parents, they might end up in a similar situation. And the situation - being trapped in a potentially evil reform school - is not a situation they want to be in.

In addition to mystery and adventure, there's some gross-out humor that young readers will likely be on board with. The prank that lands the siblings in reform school is rather disgusting: Tobias releases tadpoles into the dinner gravy, which their governess eats. This made my stomach turn rather unpleasantly - and I admit that I could have done without scenes like this - but I have no doubt many readers will find it hilarious.

This first installment leaves readers with more questions than answers and I'm curious about how the story will progress. And if the siblings will make it out of this dangerous reform school whole.

Killing Lincoln: The Shocking Assassination that Changed America Forever I have read several books which describe or include as part of the book, the history about the Lincoln assassination. I found the authors of this version to tell the story very well with colorful adjectives which does aid in the actual visualization of the events. The authors did go into excellent detail about the last days of the confederacy and in my opinion they have written this part of history better than I have read it anywhere else. However, this book was about killing Lincoln so I was at a lost as to why the authors spent so many pages on Lee's last days. There was much more mystery surrounding the events of the assassination and the days after. For example, Secretary of State's Seward's son, Frederick was described as having been hit in the head by the assassin Powell so hard that "gray matter" or part of his brain actually left his body. However, he lived to the age of 85 or so years and served as assistant Secretary of State under President's Johnson and Hayes. So the description of his injury which included his brains actually being knocked out of his head seems a bit much and screams for more information. Dr. Mud's participation is described as a foregone conclusion as to his active involvement in the assassination, however there is much written about this subject and one can say he couldn't have been anymore involved than Samuel Cox or Thomas Jones as well as Elizabeth Quesenberry's involvement which I don't recall even being touched on. I would have preferred the author's dealt more with this subject than Lee's last days. In addition the Conspiracy theory surrounding Secretary of War Stanton offered no new information although history has treated him quite kindly after the assassination. History is clear that both the North and the South offered money to cause disruption by spy's. However, the author's to me seem to imply this was different. So for me, I was under the impression this book was going to offer new evidence as to why those that aided Booth in his escape, much more so that Dr. Mudd, were not tried when people like the poor stage hand Spangler who just held Booth's horse, was tried. I would suggest if you have not read a lot about this subject, you will find the book very intriguing; however, if you have, I would describe it as a very well written review of the events.

Professor Ralph's explanation of literary forms as essential for scripture study is well reasoned and well organized.  Her clear examples demonstrating how the literary form can affect interpretation has made some of the more literal-minded uncomfortable.  It is not easy to stretch one's mind beyond the presuppositions we may have retained for some time and it may even seem sacreligious when we encounter it.  It is good to attempt an open mind when encountering a work such as this and Professor Ralph conveys the message well within the confines of orthodox teaching.  The definition of literary forms such as myth, legend, debate, allegory, and even fiction may seem to challenge our understanding of revelation and inspiration.  But our understanding probably requires focus and clarity; and Professor Ralph provides just that in this bold and mind-stretching work.  We do not have to agree with every detail in classifying particular portions of scripture but we do have to accept the possibility that there may be more than one way to view some texts.  Professor Ralph assures us that that wider lens view is not a challenge to belief in the ultimate author, who is God, but and enrichment and appreciation for His use of human instruments.

Professor Ralph begins with a clear description of oral tradition - what it is and what it is not.  In so doing, she asserts the concept that Pope Benedict XVI has asserted, the hermeneutic of continuity and community.  Scripture must be interpreted in the context of the community that collected and preserved it over the span of centuries.  This is where, I believe, she provides real value over other works such as this one.  Professor Ralph does not stop with purely literary forms but uses them to show how they are related to the community that used those forms.  In this way she avoids the pitfalls of an over-reliance on historical-critical methods that has led so many down the road of agnosticism and a hermeneutic of distrust.  Professor Ralph strikes a refreshing balance between the scientific method and faith.  The uncomfortable reader should find solace and comfort that faith is not denied but upheld in this work.

Continuing to build on the description of oral tradition, Professor Ralph gives examples of each literary form and how it grew from oral tradition, to written tradition, to edited tradition.  At the end of each chapter are questions to review and discuss, making this a wonderful tool for a study group.  One thing lacking is an index however and I found many times wanting to jump back to an earlier point and having to flip pages to find what I was looking for.  With this type of work, however, an index is a minor convenience we would rarely require.

Challenging, informative, enlightening, and orthodox.  Truly a classic work in hermeneutics for the shelf of every serious Bible student.

What struck me the most about Katie Williams` debut novel is the voice. Evie is a sixteen year old girl who reads like she's much younger -- she's awkward and naive. She doesn't have friends, though she sits with a group of girls she calls The Whisperers at lunch. She makes up stories to tell them and the lies and exaggerations roll of her tongue like truths. And it's this voice that makes THE SPACE BETWEEN TREES so magical. The voice of a girl who wants so badly to be a part of things that she lies to the father of the girl found dead in the woods. She accidentally convinces Zabet McCabe's father that she was her best friend. And when the real best friend, Hadley, finds out, she at first toys with Evie, makes her squirm, knowing that she hasn't known Zabet since they were little. Because Evie is a busser who lives on the outskirts of town in a rental home. And even though Hadley is one of the "bad girls" at school, she lives in the nice neighborhood of Hokepe Woods, walks or drives to school, and never has to worry about money.

But it's not long before Hadley and Evie develop a strange sort of friendship. Hadley convinces Evie to flirt with her crush Jonah, the college drop-out who found the body, during her morning paper route, while Jonah is out patrolling for dead animals in the trees outside Hokepe Woods. Hadley wants Evie to find the exact spot where Zabet's body was found. She wants to look for clues, to solve the murder, find out who killed the girl they had in common. And while Evie knows that Hadley isn't exactly a good friend, she agrees to almost everything. Evie follows along and helps Hadley write suspect lists and go looking in places that two teenage girls shouldn't be, because the intrigue is too much to bear for her, too.

THE SPACE BETWEEN TREES is an odd coming of age story -- it is part mystery, part drama, and absolutely a story about friendship -- even if Hadly and Zabet's friendship is not ideal, their budding relationship is incredible to watch. It is the story of first loves and disappointments, and of the violence everyone things doesn't happen in their town, to their friends, until it absolutely does. It's the story of how when tragedy happens, we are both repelled and attracted by it. And it's the story of two girls who are both brought together and torn apart by the horror of it all.

Poetically written, this is the sort of book that breaks your heart, that tears into you as you read it into the wee hours of the morning because you simply cannot put it down. I highly recommend you pick up a copy -- it's a work of beauty and a voice you will not soon forget.

And since the instructions are word heavy and lacking in diagrams, you need to just cross your fingers that it will work out in the end. You might wish you were a "tween" yourself again!

I tried the Agnes tunic dress and loved the design. There were, however, a few small problems with the pattern. There is no instruction given for how to set the sleeves. I added a row of basting stitches at the top of the sleeve cap and pulled them up to ease the cap into the armhole. This is a simple enough fix, but only if you've set a few sleeves before. This is a book that will leave one thinking about the subject of immigration long after closing the final page. I must say, the story did not meet the expected happy ending that every reader longs for in this type of story. I cannot understand how any mother could leave a child behind. But, then again, I have never tried to feed a family in a world of horrific poverty with no hope of any chance of escaping that reality, ever. This is the saddest thing I have ever read. The despair I felt got deeper the closer I got to the end as I thought "what can we as Americans do to bring about change so these horrible separations of mothers and children will never happen again?" We can't just simply shrug our shoulders and say this isn't  an American problem, it is a Latin American problem.

No matter what your view on the subject matter, this is a story that everyone needs to read. It is on one hand an adventure story of the dangers the migrants face and to think that so many are children is captivating on its own. On the other hand it is a story about love of children who will never be able to shake the feeling that the mother or father who left them behind never loved them, although the opposite is the truth.

Holger Herwig's "The Marne, 1914" actually covers considerably broader ground than just the September, 1914, Battle of the Marne.  Rather, the book closely surveys the first several weeks of World War One on the Western Front, culminating (with more of a whimper than a bang) in the famed action near the Marne River.  The focus is perhaps somewhat more on the German army than upon France (and Britain and Belgium), but the Western Allies are by no means neglected.  Both sides are shown to have committed long catalogues of errors (although the Germans ultimately were less capable of recovering from their mistakes).  The primary limitation of Herwig's book, from my perspective, is the absence of maps that clearly depict what was going on.  For a reader not intimately familiar with the geography of eastern France, at times the narrative presents a daunting barrier of unfamiliar names.  There actually are quite a few maps given, but in general they show army (and corps) postiions against a background of rivers and cities and towns labeled in very small print.  Trying to use those maps to spatially envision what the text is describing can be a frustrating task.
summary: Dense portrayal of the start of a brutal war

What a beautiful book. Books about modern day celebrities generally bore the hell out of me even if I like the person (We love you, Keith, but shut up.) but this one is up there with Just Kids by Patti Smith.  Ms Allman, along with her gift for describing things-like music-that are almost impossible to describe, writes with an honesty that borders on brutality and doesn't flinch when she hits the hard stuff like love, yearning, and the hurt that men and women inflict on each other and themselves.  At the same time, she understands or attempts to understand why they do it and is not afraid to subject herself to the same scrutiny.  She was certainly blessed/cursed with the ideal subject matter.  Among all the great guitarists who came to prominence in the sixties and seventies, Duane Allman was the only one who, for me, was as frightening as Robert Johnson, and the only one whose death felt like a profound personal loss.  Ms Allman reveals both sides of the man.  He was a visionary and a genius-someone once called him an avatar-but he was also deeply flawed and capable of disturbing cruelty and violence.  Ms Allman also shows that he was a product of his time and his experiences, especially in the gender roles that men and women in the entertainment world inhabited.  As for those who are inclined to condemn him and his bandmates for their insensitivity and excesses, I would suggest that they look at the modern celebrity worship industry before they start pointing fingers.  Ms Allman is every bit her father's daughter and I'm inclined to say that she writes like he played.  Above all, the love she feels for her father shines through her story and lifts it far above the standard rock star biography.  Again, Just Kids by Patti Smith comes to mind.  Ironically enough, she perhaps first discovered that love where many of the rest of us first found it, in Duane Allman's music.  Also, consider this.  Duane Allman, Robert Johnson, and Bill Evans were tragically flawed individuals who did a lot of damage to themselves and those who cared about them, but when that has all passed away, we're left with what really mattered, the love and the music.

Jon Katz' 'Soul of a Dog' explores a taboo question: Do animals have souls? Back to the familiar, Katz shares the daily shenanigans of the dogs, cows, goats, sheep, chickens, and Mother the murderous barn cat ("the antithesis of what people mean by souls"), who cohabit his New York farm. 'Soul' is an enjoyable read, full of humor, antidote, and personality. Katz is no activist--his human bias has not yet altogether devolved--yet he explores the question fully, even "interviewing" a minister and asking if his dog Izzy will go to heaven. With questions such as these being seriously considered, Cornell University historian Dominick LaCapra's claim that the 21st will be the "Century of the Animal" appears to be right on target.

Wonderful book. Well written, well-researched and a thoroughly enjoyable read. Having read numerous books on the India/Burma battles around Kohima, Imphal, and along the Silchar Track for personal reasons, this story smacks home. A nice lead in explaining the intricacies and subtleties of being an elephant man in a difficult climate and inhospitable terrain, and especially in explaining the characters of the elephants themselves, which are the true heroes of this book. Jim Williams wasn't the only person trying to rescue refugees during this time, however; Gyles Mackrell, a British tea planter also made attempts rescuing refugees fleeing Burma. (Google his name to see his own archived film footage to give you an idea of the almost superhuman efforts and risks Williams and he took while facing a brutal Japanese onslaught.) It's a story well worth reading, if not just for its simple pleasure, or for history's sake, but also for the fundamental purpose of a good dose of perspective in reevaluating how easy and fortunate our lives have become. I'd highly recommend this book to anyone, just as it came recommended to me. Elephants are here proved to be a breed apart, just as were all the people involved in these very dangerous exploits.

But don't stop at this book; Lt-Col. J. H. Williams' own memoir, "Elephant Bill," is the core study and primary background for Elephant Company, only in more military depth and with the dry, matter-of-fact wit so prevalent among men of such fortitude.

review_text: Amazing. One of my favorite books of Mitchell's is the early Number9Dream, where he revisits a narrative over and over, with different outcomes every time. In Slade House Mitchell is experimenting with fantasy and a bit of thriller-horror, and he does interesting things with the narrative this time too, taking wholly distinct characters nine years apart in five stories, bringing them to the same fate and place in different ways each time. The plot is like a set of Matryoshka dolls, where you discover a critical detail in each revisit. There are old characters from The Bone Clocks of which this is a follow on - Marinus makes a reappearance - and the end promises a third book. I simply cannot wait.

Though Will Mackins collection of stories from US deployments in (and training for return engagements in) Iraq and Afghanistan comes with a blurb from Phil Klay, I find it difficult not to compare Bring Out the Dog with Redeployment. Klays book has a variety of narrators, Mackins one presumably autobiographical soldier whose main function is to call in airstrikes. He also participates in raids on houses and attempts to ambush Taliban troops. Like Klays collection, there are also pained accounts of encounters back home (where returned soldiers do not feel very at home).

I remember reading the poignant tale of the drowning of a leader afraid of water, Crossing the River of No Name in the New Yorker, where the prize-winning  Kattekoppen (a vile Dutch sweet) also appeared. I feel that the prototypical New Yorker story ceases without an ending, and most of the stories in Bring Out the Dog similarly disappoint me with open endings or no endings (the stories within stories are more satisfactory in this regard and Rib Night has a satisfying punchline).

There is only one developed native character, the Iraqi boy with a mysterious black box in Yankee Two. The contempt for those ostensibly being protected continues the pattern of Vietnam War fiction. The superiority in technology of the Americans to the local insurgents has only increased since then. One side has night-vision goggles, lasers, and air supportnot the side that seems to be winning the wars. Mackins narrator is quite tech savvy, though the elements of camaraderie and frustration at not being able easily to distinguish insurgents from civilians are more focal.

The stories I found most impressive include one set in the Utah Test and Training Range (The Fire Truck), one set on a base dining hall (Rib Night), one involving fictive kin of an Afghan translator (Remain Over Day), the aforementioned apprehended Iraqi boy in Yankee Two, and two elegies for fallen comrades: a canine one in Great Circle Westward through Perpetual Night), Hal in Crossing the River of No Name.

Gallows humor is sprinkled across the volume. There are no stories that I found uninteresting, but others are less fully realized than those I mentioned, and few solidly land endings. The prose is mostly straightforward (Hemingways influence lives on!) with dollops of surrealism and some reaching for (without always grabbing onto) metaphors.
summary: Going off to see the world with high-tech equipment and an opaque overall mission

review_text:
Ever since I've read Mellenthin's Panzer Battles I was intrigued by Hermann Balck.  And then I encountered his name when the American ground forces were getting bogged down around Metz in late 44.  And with how Mellenthin and others described him, I was dying to read his memoirs, but sadly they were not translated into English.  When I found out this book was finally coming out I was so happy.

I really like his writing style, his pre WW2 experiences are just as fascinating (perhaps almost more fascinating) over his WW2 experiences.

The best portions are the book is when he discusses his view of tactics, operations, and strategy and the idea of an active defense.  But the unexpectedly surprise of the book was his opinion and views of Hitler.  Very opposed to almost every other views of Hitler you will read about in other memoirs.  He argues that Hitler interfered very little with his command, that Hitler was right many many times when it came to his decisions, and that at the end of the war Hitler was still very competent and not insane.

You don't see that opinion expressed anywhere.  Is Balck trying to write fiction in that regards for some purpose?  Or is he countering Guderian, Manstein, and many others who simply blame Hitler for everything and are fudging the truth?

Phillip E. Johnson (born 1940) is a retired UC Berkeley law professor and a co-founder of the Discovery Institute's Center for Science and Culture, and is one of the leading figures in the Intelligent Design movement. He has also written books such as Darwin on Trial,Reason in the Balance: The Case Against Naturalism in Science, Law and Education,Objections Sustained: Subversive Essays on Evolution, Law and Culture,The Wedge of Truth: Splitting the Foundations of Naturalism, etc. He wrote in the Introduction to this 1997 book, "This book grew out of two conversations. The first was... with ... my usual publisher. The [InterVarsity] Press was ready for me to do another book, but I wasn't sure I was ready... however, it became clear that there was ONE book I needed to write very soon... There was clearly a need for a short book aimed at ... [those] not quite so familiar with university-level subjects. In particular, I wanted to write for late teens... That brings me to the second conversation, which occurred in the faculty club of my own university... [I realized that] If high-schoolers need a good high-school education in how to think about evolution, professors and senior scientists seem to need it just as badly. That's what this book aims to give---a good high-school education in how to think about evolution." (Pg. 9-11) He comments about the Scopes "Monkey Trial": "Darrow did not want to balance the Bible with evolutionary science; he wanted to get rid of religion and replace it with science and agnostic philosophy. On the other hand, [William Jennings] Bryan truly was a scientific ignoramus, and the wily Darrow really did make a fool out of him. If Darrow had wanted, he probably could just as easily have made the leading evolutionary scientists of the day look foolish. For example, some of these scientists confidently cited the fraudulent Piltdown Man and the tooth of 'Nebraska Man' (which turned out to be from a kind of pig) as proof of human evolution. If Bryan was confused about the evidence for evolution, he had a lot of respectable company." (Pg. 29) He argues, "Think how much pressure the other physical anthropologists are under to develop standards that will allow SOME fossils to be authenticated as human ancestors... why do you think such a high proportion of the fossils used to prove 'evolution' come from this one specialty? Why do you think Niles Eldredge, a specialist in marine invertebrates, uses hominid examples rather than the vast record of fossil invertebrates to argue the case for evolution?" (Pg. 62) He observes, "Most readers of this book probably don't feel qualified to judge scientific disputes. For that matter, Richard Dawkins ] himself is a zoologist and not a biochemist, and he told me himself that he doesn't feel qualified to debate [Michael] Behe's scientific claims ]." (Pg. 79) He adds, "Behe is a Roman Catholic who has no religious objection to Darwinian evolution; his argument is simply that the Darwinian mechanism has no scientific merit in molecular biology. Neither [critic] contradicted Behe on any scientific point. Their objections were entirely philosophical, or based on a failure to comprehend the concept of design." (Pg. 80) Those who enjoy Johnson's other books will surely enjoy this (unless they are looking for a MORE "detailed" presentation, which is admittedly not his aim in this book).

Joslin "Josh" McDowell (born 1939) is a Christian author best known for his many works of apologetics; he has been affiliated with Campus Crusade for Christ (now "Cru") since 1964. His many books include Evidence that Demands a Verdict: Historical Evidence for the Christian Faith,More Evidence That Demands a Verdict,Daniel in the Critics' Den,The Islam Debate,The Resurrection Factor,Josh McDowell Answers Five Tough Questions, etc. His life story was told in Joe Musser's book Josh: Excitement of the Unexpected and also in the DVD Undaunted. Josh's first two books were material used for his lectures, etc., and were filled with long quotations, which often covered the same ground; they weren't exactly the sort of book that a Christian would hand to a non-Christian and say, "Here, read this," as the non-Christian would probably get "lost" in the quotations, or the complex and technical discussions of Volume II. This 1977 book precisely fills that gap. [There was also a VHS tape of the same name released by Johnson/Nyquist Productions, but it's no longer available.] He begins by asking, "How is Jesus different from other religious leaders? Why don't the names of Buddha, Mohammed, Confucius offend people? The reason is that these others didn't claim to be God, but Jesus did. That is what makes him so different from other religious leaders... He was presenting himself as the only avenue to a relationship with God, the only source of forgiveness for sins, and the only way of salvation." (Pg. 10) He adds, "Jesus received honor and worship that only God should receive... Jesus received worship as God (Matt 14:33, 28:9) and sometimes even demanded to be worshipped as God (John 5:23...)." (Pg. 12) He recalls that a professor once asserted to him that "Mark, the earliest Gospel, never once mentioned Jesus' claiming to be God... In response I turned to Mark's Gospel. There Jesus claimed to be able to forgive sins... By Jewish law this was something only God could do; Isaiah 43:25 restricts this prerogative to God alone... we can forgive injuries committed against us, but in no way can anyone forgive sins committed against God except God himself. That is what Jesus did." (Pg. 18-19) He countered another professor's assertion that "the New Testament was written so long after Christ that it could not be accurate in what it recorded" by saying, "By the twentieth century... archaeological discoveries had confirmed the accuracy of the New Testament manuscripts. Discoveries of early papyri manuscripts [the John Ryland manuscript, A.D. 130; the Chester Beatty Papyri, A.D. 155; and the Bodmer Papyri II, A.D. 200) bridged the gap between the time of Christ and existing manuscripts from a later date." (Pg. 42) The book (as did Volume I of "Evidence") concludes with Josh's moving testimony. Josh has written many other books, including several which cover this material in much greater detail ,He Walked Among Us]; but as the most "readable" introduction to Josh's apologetic, this smaller book can hardly be beaten.

First off, I am a huge fan of the Oxmoor House/Southern Living line of cookbooks.  This one has me a bit conflicted.  Cookies are not an essential part of living.  They are a treat, they are an indulgence and they can be creatively personalized fun.  Because of all of those things a cookbook featuring this treat should be bright and cheerful.  Unfortunately for me this book just didn't meet that expectation.  Don't get me wrong, the cookie recipes are absolutely wonderful, but the styling of the photographs is not.

The Recipes:  I've read through the entire cookbook and found exactly what I would expect from a Southern Living cookbook in the form of a variety of recipes with helpful hints on which quality ingredients and utensils to have on hand to give you optimum results.  I really love the fact that the ingredient list is separate away from the instructions and the photograph for each recipe.  I like the feature called "Cookie Swap" which gives hints on how to switch out ingredients for that particular cookie to give variety to the recipe.  I love that there is a separate photograph of each finished cookie.  On looking through the recipes I recognize many of the recipes I already consider old favorites except with a different name or slightly different ingredients.  I've tried four recipes already - I was actually making out a grocery list the day this book arrived in the mail so planned my shopping list for two recipes immediately - and all four have turned out really well.  Just as I would have expected.  These are the four I've made so far:  Chocolate-Dipped Toffee-Pecan Cookies, Browned Butter Pecan Shortbread, Lemon Cheesecake Bars, and Praline Bars.  There is also a recipe for Small Batch Cream Cheese Frosting that is going to come in very handy.  I took the Lemon Cheesecake Bars and the Praline Bars to a party last night and there wasn't even a crumb left.  That's high recommendation indeed.

The Presentation:  Because of the styling decisions made for presenting the finished product, this cookbook is "dark".  That's not what I want to see in a cookie cookbook.  I've noticed this trend in cookbooks for a while now and it sometimes works for other food but definitely not for cookies.  The surfaces the cookies are placed on are either old, dark wood or an old galvanized type metal surface.  The containers the cookies are placed or stacked in are old worn cookie sheets, dark buckets, old metal dishes or old metal pans.  Often the cookies are displayed on the parchment paper they were baked on and that has turned a dark brown.  The utensils shown as dressing for the finished products are old and dark and worn out looking.  There is even one sifter I would be afraid to put any ingredients in to sift because it looks like flecks of metal might end up in my flour.  No......I'm sorry Southern Living, this was a mistake and people simply picking up the book and thumbing through it will (in my opinion) be more likely to put it back down and walk away.  The book itself is plenty large enough to have lots of space for the ingredients list and instructions.  It has a paper-board kind of cover so you can pretty easily make the book stay open to the page you are working from.

So the quandary I find myself in is deciding on a star rating based on the recipes I've tried and the ones I want to try or based on the overall impression upon simply looking through the book.  The recipes would automatically be five stars if that was all I had to consider.  I've settled on four stars because the recipes are well presented and, so far, have turned out well plus I'm taking the reputation of Oxmoor House and Southern Living into consideration.  By all means use the 'look inside' feature on Amazon to get a sneak peek at what you will be getting if you decide to buy this cookbook.  As I said, not a single crumb remained from the two batches I took to the party.  That counts for a lot!
summary: This cookbook has me a bit conflicted.

review_text:
John Trent PhD and Gary Smalley's book THE BLESSING has been around for decades. This reprint is an attempt to generate interest and sales in the title again. I checked on the Net, and they have websites set up all over the place, to work along with the book. The pop Psychology within the book was composed on shakey grounds, as far as serious psychology goes, but the theological underpinings used as biblical support for the ideas on child rearing doesnt even quote the bible correctly half the time. In a nutshell, if you bless your child, meaning give the child "MEANINGFUL TOUCH", "A SPOKEN MESSAGE", "ATTACH HIGH VALUE TO THE CHILD", "PICTURE A HAPPY FUTURE", and provide an "ACTIVE COMMITMENT", then the child will be blessed, and function as a happy Christian, and good parent. It seemed like a lot of pink clouds when I read the theory, but I was game, and wanted to see HOW you could get parents to instill love uncondistionally, to create psychologically perfect children. Of course, if a parent WITHHOLDS a blessing, then the child might as well go buy the heroin, guns and porn, cos the child is CURSED. (I'm not joking.) The Blessing is seen as parental acceptence, with uncondistional love. Naturally, if you have a premise that far out, its up to the bible to PROVE you're right. These biblical proofs of their theory, is where the book falls apart. The writers point out a famous Biblical person, who was withhelt his father's blessing, much to their mutual distress. ISAAC and REBEKAH had twins, Esau and Jacob. Isaac, like his father Abraham, were tribal leaders, and the selection of the next tribal leader was given thru a blessing. Esau was the oldest of the twins, but Jacob was persuaded by his mother to trick his blind father, to recieve the blessing, and become the tribal leader of the earliest jews. IMPORTANT--JACOB WAS NOT WITHHOLDING HIS LOVE FROM ESAU. In fact, Jacob was furious when he discovered the subterfuge played on him, as was Esau. (since he wouldnt get to be the "king".) Nowhere is it even SUGGESTED that Esau wasn't loved, etc. Yet on the twisted belief that Esau was "WITHHELT THE BLESSING" all children deserve, this lack of the blessing for Esau made him bitter, sad, ultimately hating his brother. However, Jacob DOES give a blessing to Esau (Gen 27:39)saying that he would in time shake off his yoke, and win back his freedom. Anyway, Jacob stayed away from Esau for years, then returned to his homeland a rich man. Jacob gave Esau a King's reward, and they were good brothers again. SO, how do these two authors base an entire theory of Sibling rivalry, and parental favortism, from a withhelt blessing, from that story?

THE BLESSING then expounds this idea that Parents CURSE their children, if they don't bless them utilizing the five point program outlined in the book. Right there red flags start waving. These psychologists remove the role of genetics in determining behaviors in children, as well as enviormental factors outside the influence of parents and homelife. Pop psychology oftens oversimplifies a premise, in order to make it easily understood by the masses for whom the "theory" has ultimately been tailored for. If you look at the lives of saints, some are treated horriblely by their parents, yet are holy and blessed.(Saint Dymphna) Others are raised by parents who constantly pray for their children, yet the temptations of the world lead them on the wrong path.(St. Augustine's early life). Psychology isn't black and white like this. Even ONE SCIENTIFIC STUDY proving that children raised with talented siblings receiving extra parental attention don't feel as loved, is not to be found. Condensed antidotal stories is the only "science" to be found. For example, a young girl watches horror films with her dad, while he has a few beers. He calls her by some pet name, like Lady Dracula, something like that. According to the authors, this behavior produced a 16 year old girl who WEARS BLACK CLOTHES in hot weather, because she is "GOTH". AND, therefore not christian. There is also much banter based on communicating with "word pictures". THis is another pop psychology myth from the 80s--that the right hemisphere of the brain works in pictures, and it contains the emotional content, while the left brain is about words and logic. THe authors believe that men use their left brain, and women use their right, so that is the root of miscommunication. So the book diverges into these ideas, so you know HOW you are to effectively communicate with your spouse or children, in order to further your blessing potentials. IF that's not confusing enough, the authors have all these websites for showing your how to raise your children with the Blessing. (Faith @ Home).

The writers suggest the insecurity problem with kids is dealt with thru giving lots of hugs. After saying that good touch, kissing, hugs, etc also bestows the blessing, the authors finally give us some scientific information. Here it is--in Puerto Rico people touch about 180 times an hour (once every 20 seconds), whereas in London, they touch ZERO times per hour, and in FLorida people touch twice an hour. They make the connection, that the USA is a country filled with child abuse and molesting, because we are not constantly touching and hugging each other. (But they don't say whether or not there is child abuse and molesting in Puerto Rico,even tho they have all those blessing touches. So unfortunately they misuse the scientific method again.) I could go on, and talk about how horrible it is to suggest to children, that they have been cursed by parents who didn't touch them enough, but it would just upset me. IT's obvious, that the REAL paternal blessing comes from our Divine Father.  Parents are not perfect people. To expect any parent to love UNCONDISTIONALLY, and raise kids perfectly equal, could make a parent neuroticallly hypervigilant. (and no doubt the children as well.) A parent is only expected to love their children, and raise them as best they can. Very little is based on psychological studies, outside of a few anecdotal "case studies" in THE BLESSING, never more than a page or two long. The authors tend to over emphesize some common mistake, like calling a child with learning disabilities a "slow learner", as the way the parent CURSES the child. (Using this book to convince you your parents cursed you, because they told you you might be limited in some way, is harmful to a child's respect and confidence in the wisdom of their parents, and could cause terrible guilt to the parents.) I'm not saying this book has no value. I'm not convinced that a parent "blessing" a child in this five step program, is the "be all and end all" for raising mentally healthy, spiritually mature children. For that matter, suggesting that if you DONT follow this program, you might end up CURSING your child, has got to be a bad mind game to throw on anyone...parent or child. Suggesting that not getting the same amount of hugs, etc, means that your parents have FLOODED one child with blessings, and made a desert of blessings for the other child, sounds like a bad idea too. Even with the added help given with the internet sites that are set up to help you implement this 5 step program, I don't believe the wisdom doiled out in this book, will do much more than brainwash your kids, or make them neurotic. Sometimes, its best to have faith in GOD, and let him handle giving us our blessings.

The first thing that struck me about Mr. Leehan's writing was its bluntness. There are very few Christian authors out there that speak in terms that are understood by the secular world or even those who are Christians. His is not a tale of someone's "fall from Grace" but a stark, gritty, and shocking story of a revolt against that Grace.

Most of us are only vaguely aware of the invisible war going on around us in the form of God and good versus Satan and evil. In Leehan's book we get a front row seat in the theatre as he describes his conscious rebellion against a God he didn't understand. Angry and depressed with how his life is going Leehan actually declares his allegiance to Satan and so begins a most horrific and amazing journey.

The thing that amazes me most about Michael's story is just how patient and forgiving God is and how He can take any situation and use it for his Glory. This book is a shocking reminder of just how far Satan is willing to go to keep each and every one of us away from the Kingdom. Even to the extent of walking the aisles of our own churches.

One of the most interesting passages in the book talks about how Satan preys on new believers by infiltrating Bible studies and targeting the weak; the people who haven't established themselves in their faith and get them to sin. In so doing an imaginary rift is created between them and God that is filled with shame. Often this causes the person to cease all connection with the church out of shame and guilt; A huge wake-up call to all pastors and leaders.

As Christians we need to be aware of the war we are in and be prepared to fight in that war daily. Leehan's book clearly and graphically gives us an inside look at the tactics used to separate us from God. I recommend reading it but be warned, it is not an easy read. Do so prayerfully and carefully.
summary: A Wake Up Call to Christians

This is a great book for those Christians struggling with understanding the government and how to think and act Christ-like to those in authority.

MacArthur gives a Christian perspective on the government and political involvement. He discusses the purpose of government and the Christian's responsibility toward it.

MacArthur also teaches in this "Bible For Life" series about the Christian's obligation toward taxes. Basically, Christians are to pay their taxes. He demonstrates this with Jesus' teaching on taxes.

Of course, no book like this would be complete without a couple of examples from the Bible. MacArthur uses the example of Daniel and Paul to show how a Christian should live and interact (maybe even be a part of the government) with the government and its authorities.

Christians are to support their leaders and obey them, provided the leaders are not giving orders in direct violation of God's Word. Finally, there is a chapter about how to live in a pagan society.

There is also a sermon from Charles Haddon Spurgeon at the end of the book about Citizenship in Heaven. The book includes a study guide for group study or further individual reflection.

True to MacArthur's style, this book is filled with scriptural references. I highly recommend this book for anyone to read. This is this best book I have ever read about how a Christian should respond and deal with their government.
summary: Great book on a difficult topic.

I had the privilege of hearing Leonard Sweet, the author of "I Am A Follower: The Way, Truth and Life of Following Jesus"  in college. I remember thinking that this man is not only smart but he makes me want to know Jesus differently. He was engaging, thoughtful and focused on teaching true biblical messages. His core message in this book is the idea that we are called as Christians to follow Jesus, not to be leaders.

One of the most poignant remarks that Sweet makes in his book is the notion that our church leaders (i.e. pastors, deacons, etc) have become lords in the church, something that Christ taught against:

"Those who fill the roles of pastors or elders are meant to be nothing more than disciplined and discipled fellow followers who are committed to a life of serving with and within and alongside Christ's body" (pg. 178).

This certainly is a different approach to thinking about Christianity. Perhaps, our world has distorted what it means to follow Jesus so much that we have made it acceptable or been purposeful in leading rather then following.

I will admit that Sweet's book is heavy. It is a heavy read. He is an incredibly smart individual and I think he struggles with making some aspects a bit more elementary. I doubt he even recognizes the need to simplify things but for someone like me rather new in my faith, it would be refreshing to have some things explained. However, I do not doubt that this book would be an excellent read for individuals in various stages of faith.

I also believe that this book provides great resource for students or individuals in organizational leadership. It is a different way of thinking about "leading" and I believe it will be worth the time spent to read. I highly recommend this for believers who want to deepen their faith and examine how they walk with Jesus.

The conversation I've dreamed of since I first read Max Lucado just took place. In written form, of course.

After 25 years of writing books, with more than fifty to his credit so far, Max held a question and answer session. Not about himself, personally, but about his God, and what he continues to learn about him to this day. Those raising the burning questions come from varied backgrounds; from not-yet Christians to lifelong church goers, from worn out debates to brand new possibilities, from the youngest of children to the most experienced in life. People asked, and Max did his best to answer.

I appreciate the type of book that allows you to search for something in particular, but keeps you turning pages longer than you first intended. This could be considered a research book, preparing the reader for pelting from a doubting world. This could be considered a spiritual growth book, allowing the reader to rest in the fact that the message has never changed, and that scripture truly answers each question. This could be considered a book of preparation for anyone wishing to enter a ministry, because it addresses the issues that caring, hurting people carry around with them. If someoen ever hopes to reach an audience, then understanding the heart of that audience is an important first step.

Most important, this is the type of book my 17-year-old daughter might pull off the shelf when confronted by one of her Atheist friends, or another teen who is struggling with finding a way to matter in a world that clearly says they do not. When she searches for answers, this will help her find them, or at least show her where to start.

Max offers as much truth as possible, mixed with his careful opinion in areas where the Bible may be silent. He treats the questions with respect, acknowledging the fact that it's the questions that force him to dig deeper. He never claims to have all the answers; but in his own personal attempt to find them, he shares insight that makes sense, his growing knowledge from his constant journey. I sense that had he written this book at the beginning of his years as an author and minister, it would have a very different outcome. The same is true if he tackles these same questions 25 years from now.

For me, the greatest value of this book was found at the end; a seven-page addendum entitled The Write Stuff. He never simplifies the process, but shares why he continues to write, to find new words to express God's story. He shares his struggles with the editing process, but admits that his words are better because of it. "Writing is not glamorous work. But it is noble, holy, and worthwhile," Max shares, spurring his readers on to share their story in a written word if there is no way to silence it.

I highly recommend this book, especially if you like to learn by doing.  This is a workbook oriented book.  Within the first few pages, you will make a simple frame loom (if you do not already have a tapestry loom), find a few easy to find materials, and you begin making your weave along sampler.  Instead of having to digest a few chapters before getting hands on, you are hands on almost immediately.  But the author does not skimp on illustrations, photos, or detailed instructions.  After the sampler, you will move on to more progressively detailed products that you will be proud to display, rather than stuff in a drawer or box of "first attempts".  After the sampler, the projects include:
A gorgeous sun sampler that you will want to hang on your wall.  This sampler goes back over what you learned in the first introductory sampler, but adds additional detail and is a little more technical, and the result is a fresh update on those somber toned tapestries of the 1970's.  Next, a peruvian inspired bird tapestry with bead and feather trim; a cat and fishes tapestry; a simple beach landscape; the tree tapestry that is also the cover illustration; instructions for warp and weft variations; using bright color and shades of grey; instructions for weaving from the side; suggestions for using what you've learned to design your own tapestries; an owl sampler; a colorful sleeping dog sofa cushion; equally colorful sleeping cat and bird sofa cushions; finishing, framing and mounting techniques, and as if you haven't already had enough  eye candy as you've been working along with the author, a gallery of even more inspiring work.  By the time you have finished working through this book, you will be past the beginning weaver stage and into intermediate designing and weaving.  Ms. Glasbrook has packed a lot of information into the 96 pages of this book.  This book is not every thing you will need/want to know about tapestry weaving, but this book gives you a very solid foundation.
summary: You'll be weaving in no time

First, a comment on the e-book quality of "Camille" - good but not great, only 2 or 3 typos, excellent formatting, but no page numbers - just the wacky % read and minutes left, etc.

 As for the novel, it's great !  A fitting conclusion to a wonderful trilogy. Unfortunately, the US publisher (?) released the second book of the series first, and this is a series that MUST be read in order, so do yourself a favor and get "Irene" as fast as you can - you are in for a great treat.  Pay attention to all the members of Police Commandant Camille Verhoeven's team - they are critical, popping up in all of the books.  Throughout the series but perhaps best in Alex, book 2, Le Maitre comes up with the most timely, surprising, and natural of all twists - so much better than the token turns concocted by just about every crime fiction writer.  And his prose is excellent, as usual.

All crime fiction writers create their protagonists burdened by a major character flaw - it must be rule #1 of crime fiction writing 101.  Many deal with alcohol addiction, others a drug problem, still others a medical condition, etc., etc.  Verhoeven's baggage is truly unique, one that you don't forget while reading the story, but rather something that you come to accept as you get to know and admire the character.  A small example of LeMaitre's genius, you might say.  The stories take place in Paris, always charming, and a nice plus. The stories are tight, and maintain a satisfying level of tension throughout.

"Camille" begins with a violent jewelry store robbery.  (There is a fair bit of violence in each of the books, but only a splash of blood and gore, with a tad more in "Alex" as I recall.)  Normally, not the Commandant's thing - but someone close to him happens to be at the wrong place at the wrong time and suffers for it.  Camille concocts a story, and the case is his.  But like the other two books it soon becomes apparent that everything is not as simple as it first appears and we are soon exposed to other layers, and more layers.

The climax is most fitting (major portions of Paris DO NOT get destroyed) though not the fairy tale ending some of us would like.  But there's still room for a future Verhoeven book.  I doubt it but I will keep checking for number 4.....
summary: Read this great trilogy; you must start with book one -  Irene

I found the characters to be entertaining and fun to read and Nora didn't annoy me as many female characters seem to do in paranormal YA. When I finished Hush, Hush I couldn't wait to read Crescendo.

Its unfortunate that I did not enjoy Crescendo nearly as much as I did its predecessor. There was still mystery, and danger, and Vee who had made herself onto the bad best friend's list in the later half of Hush, Hush redeemed herself in Crescendo (an unexplained 180 but I'll take it). Vee was funny, dependable and someone I wouldn't mind spending time with which made it all the more easier for me to not like Nora. I found Nora to be needy, "too stupid to live" and just basically irritating and because Nora was the narrator for the story she really ruined the book for me. Patch was basically a complete mystery for most of this book he has secrets that he can't share with Nora which makes her suspect the worse and accuse him of the worse which I could not understand because Patch, despite having his secrets, was always there for Nora, constantly pulling her out of the trouble she deliberately puts herself in.

We learn a lot more about angel and nephillim dynamics, there is more character development when it comes to side characters like Rixon and Marcie Millar and as I got more answers there were a lot more questions for me to ask.

I love Philippa Gregory. I love the Cousin's War series: The White Queen, The Lady of the Rivers, and The Red Queen are so strong and compelling that I couldn't wait to read The White Princess (the conclusion of the series.)
 But - I was disappointed by TWP. While reading the other three books in the series, I was eager to get back into the story on my lunch breaks and before bed. I didn't necessarily feel this way with TWP.

My main gripe with this novel is that as a stand alone, it's weak. Compared to the rest of the series, it does not match up. What makes it weak? Repetition. Repetition. Repetition. I just felt like the same descriptions, lines of dialogue, and character arc (ish?? Do the characters ever really change?) just repeated and stalled. What also makes this novel different to the others in the series is that Elizabeth of York is not as strong of a protagonist as Elizabeth Woodville, Margaret Beaufort, or Jacquetta Woodville. Rather than making things happen like the latter three, Elizabeth of York lets things happen to her. Now, I completely understand the historical context - as a woman, she only had so much power and Gregory had to work within set out historical facts. That being said, this is historical fiction. Gregory often points out that her work is fiction and that people should not take it as fact. So if it's historical fiction, make Elizabeth of York more fiery or defiant or even proactive - all within the confines of historical fact (i.e. conversations behind closed doors, not recorded by history.)

I find it hard to believe that Elizabeth of York apparently "grows to love' Henry VII - a man who, as Gregory has fictionalized, raped Elizabeth while they were betrothed. A man who was her family's enemy. A man who is cold and suspicious of her throughout the entire novel. I found myself getting so fed up of Henry's constant accusations of Elizabeth, and whether that was on purpose to make the reader feel how Elizabeth felt, I don't know. But it was off putting.

There were parts that I enjoyed. Perhaps the most interesting part of the book was when "the boy" and Katherine Huntly come to court - but that happens in the last third! And then the book just kind of ends abruptly.

I won't tell anyone to avoid this book because I believe everyone has different tastes. But from a prose and structure point of view - Philippa Gregory has proved she can do better. Maybe there were pressures from her publishing house to complete a new book in a smaller time frame. Even the cover image doesn't seem up to par with the others. Because I know Gregory can do better, I'm going to chalk TWP up to the money-hungry/business end of all this.
summary: We know PG can do better

The premise of this book is good: an EMP takes out most of the US (maybe the world?), and those that aren't dead either go primal or have to fight to stay alive. Alex has gone on a last trip in the woods to take care of some family business before the "monster" in her head gets her. She's out camping in the woods by herself when people start dying or turning in crazy cannibal people. Through a series of harrowing encounters, she meets two companions who end up going with her to find a place away from the crazy people, and they stay together for about the first half of the book. Alex is on her own at the start of the second half of the book, when she finds a town full of people who weren't affected the EMP that wrecked havoc at the beginning. She starts to learn that the town isn't all that it seems, and the book leaves off with Alex in a very dangerous situation.

I really liked the action in this book. Bick was not afraid to include the gory details, and this made the story seem much more real. There were several times I gripped my Kindle so hard my fingers turned white, which I think is very telling of how involved I got in the story. I felt like I could relate to Alex, even though I've never been in even a remotely similar situation with her medical condition or the things she has to deal with. She's strong, and even though she can't do everything, she doesn't just stand by and let others do things for her (like characters in other books I've read). Alex also grows in her relationships with her two companions, and I found myself rooting for them all.

However, I felt like there was no real story arc to this book. Rather, it felt like a lead-in to the second book more than a story within an overall story. That's fine, it just never feels like anything is resolved, and I'm not usually a fan of that type of book. Alex makes friends only for them to essentially disappear with no explanation halfway through the book. Then she makes new friends only to have other things happen with no resolution. I felt like that's what the book was about: things happen and never get resolved. I'm sure there's an overall plan for these situations in future books, but there could have at least been ONE resolution in this one.

Overall, I thought Ashes was a good read. I'll be reading the second book when it comes out. I've read better, less frustrating one's, though.

After being excited about "American Assassin," (I gave it four stars), I was looking forward to reading the next story in the prequel series of Mitch Rapp's career.  Unfortunately, "Kill Shot" wasn't as good as its predecessor--nor as good as the originals.

"Kill Shot" didn't have a lot of action, wasn't very suspenseful, and contained few surprises.  Yes, Vince Flynn still impresses with his knowledge of spycraft, but at this point we're pretty used to that.  And of course this one suffers from the same thing "American Assassin"--and any prequel--does.  That is, a knowledge that the recurring character is in no danger of death.  What can make a prequel work, however, is character development.  Here, we get little of it.  It's just a story of a job Rapp was to take care of that goes wrong.

Rapp's got a hit list and in this one, he's to take out the Libyan oil minister.  He does this, but rather rudely finds out there are others there too--and they're there to take Rapp out.  So Rapp's not sure how he got sold out and suspects anyone and everyone from Kennedy, to Stansfield, to Hurley, to Hurley's bulldog of an agent Victor.  The bulk of the book is Rapp trying to figure out who's after him.  Meanwhile, we find out others at Langley are trying to work their way up the ladder in a rather treasonous way.

There is obviously at least one more book in the prequel series but I'm not holding out much hope it'll be good.  At this point, it's basically going to be a revenge-type sequel.  Been there, done that. I think Flynn needs to take a break from Rapp and find another character to create.  Don't misunderstand; Flynn's great at what he does.  But the Rapp character has played out--actually quite some time ago.  I think Flynn was hoping to discover more about Rapp by going back in time, but it's not worked out very well here.

I also feel I need to comment on the fact that we're not really told when this is occurring.  While I understand this book takes place not long after the events of "American Assassin," I also know I can't remember specifics a year after reading a book.  It's obviously pre-9/11, but new readers might not know this--especially if they've not read "American Assassin." review_text:
This review is for the entire seven-volume series, which must be read in order. I'm going to post it for each book, without variation, so no need to read it more than once.

None of the books stands alone. I'd guess the total word count approaches 2 million, which is 15-20 conventional novels. It took me 7-and-a-half weeks to read, but I'm not a fast reader. The setting is modeled on medieval Europe in the Ottonian age (10th century) and does a good job of it in the context of the fantasy elements. The story follows people who are themselves nobility or who serve and regularly interact with the nobility. This is, like its analog, a world centered on secular dynasties that intermarry entirely for political reasons and on a deeply rooted religious culture (where many younger sons and daughters are parked with or without any vocation). Sorcery is forbidden, but it is practiced by some even so.

The plot is extremely complex, and there are several point-of-view characters we follow through all seven volumes. There are three main villains; I found one of them quite entertaining, despite her despicable acts of black magic, because she has talked herself into believing that everything she does is for the sake of religious purity rather than her own lust for power.

Early on, I wanted to shake the lead female character to put some sense into her (she is very young at the start), but I enjoyed her growth into self knowledge and watching her learn how to harness her power (it's fantasy, I know, but I still find that the tale of her origins strains credulity). Interesting that I found only one character completely likable (Rosvita).

Rather than summarize the plot, I'll point out some other likes and dislikes.

Likes
How the religious heresy develops and spreads (in a reversal of Christian orthodoxy and heterodoxy); some of this is comical, given who is doing the spreading
Pursuit of knowledge as something some characters desire above all else.
Rosvita (the best of the secondary leads)
Development of the longstanding consequences of Alain's early act of compassion.
The faithful hounds
Women have agency and men can be victims of a powerful woman's lust (truer in the real world than in most fiction).
Wolfhere (a mysterious non-POV character who is close to a tragic figure).

Dislikes
Too much time and detail on the astrology. Yes, it's central, but a little went a long way. I sympathized with the characters who rolled their eyes over it.
The other seven sleepers. This never really went anywhere.
The Heleniad, Augustina, Gregoria, and so onamusing a time or two; after that, insistence on female analogs just got tiresome (no problem with them being females; just thought the name game was silly)
Romanticizing primitive lifestyles (the Adica storyline and the Ashioi). One, I don't buy the noble savage and two, once was enough.

On the whole, I liked the series, but it does require a considerable investment of time.
summary: Series is one long book in seven volumes, but it's worth the time.

This book was first published in 1980 and revised in 1981.  It is a very thoughtful and thought-provoking book yet very readable.  It is about the trend in America away from an orthodox Christian world view, towards a humanist world view.  Humanists are pushing the Christian world view out of government, out of schools, out of the public square.  Liberal Christians are humanists who dress up their humanism in Christian language.  On the cover flap, it says it is literally a call for Christians to change the course of history  by returning to biblical Truth and by allowing Christ to be the Lord in all of life.  I didn't realize it at first, but it is really targeted at American Christians, more than Christians in other countries.

I should explain what the humanist world view is.  Sometimes Schaeffer calls it the material-energy chance view, or some variation of that.  It sees that the universe consists of material and energy and everything happens by chance.  It doesnt leave room for God as creator and ruler.  When it is called humanist or humanism, attention is drawn to the idea that man is at the center, not God.  Often it includes the concept of the Perfectability of Man.  It does not recognize God as a higher authority and as a source of law.

Humanists do not see that law is subordinate to God, so they can enact any law they wish.  For example, they can make abortion legal.  In the colonial days, and the early days of our republic, government acknowledged God.  The Declaration of Independence acknowledged God, or our Creator.  A Presbyterian minister, John Witherspoon, signed the Declaration of Independence.  Some of the colonies, and some of the states, had established churches.  The First Amendment says that the federal government cannot have an established church, and the federal government cannot interfere with the free practice of religion.  (p 34-35)  Today the First Amendment is used by humanists to silence the church and remove religion as an influence in civil government and education.  Schaeffer sees that democratic, limited government, with checks and balances, could only have originated in a country where Reformation Christians were in the majority.

Writing in 1980 and 1981, Schaeffer saw an open window with Ronald Reagan elected President.  It was possible to push back the influence and power of the humanists.  But he was not sure that this window would bring success.  He considered the limits of civil obedience and the options of civil disobedience and force as a response to a humanist government that had abrogated its right to govern.  A Christian must consider civil disobedience as a possible option in certain conditions, or else the government has replaced God as the highest authority.  Schaeffer does not advocate civil disobedience as some kind of lunatic fringe rebel.  He does this in a careful, reasoned, thoughtful way, taking care to not let his writing to be misused.

I thought the book ended abruptly. I was expecting something more. I think some more real world examples requiring civil disobedience or force would have helped.  There is discussion of abortion in quite a few chapters.  This is not a real good example, because the current law does not compel anyone, any Christian, to disobey God.  It just allows people to have abortions without government prosecution.  In Jesus day, the government allowed people to disobey God in many ways, and Jesus did not take his case to the government, he told the people to be obedient.  There are lots of Gods commandments that the government does not attempt to enforce, not just abortion.  So these are loose ends that Schaeffer just does not tie up.  But it is still a very good, important book.

Schaeffer died in 1984.  One wonders what he would think of America today.  Surely he would be disappointed in the advance of humanism and its progress in overpowering the orthodox Christian world view.  But he would be heartened by the pockets of resistance that still exist.

In "Final Flight," author Peter Stekel briefly brings to life four young men who died more than 60 years ago. These young aviators had volunteered to serve their country in the tumultuous early days of World War II, and died during a training mission. Their aircraft, and their bodies, came to rest on a glacier in the High Sierra, and several mysteries began.

Stekel, who has spent a lifetime in the High Sierra, began following the story of these young men when a body was discovered in 2005. He drew upon personal knowledge of the area and innate tenacity to puzzle out a reasonable explanation of why the crash occurred, and why it took place where it did. In the abstract, his plausible solutions make for an interesting read.

However, "Final Flight" is much more personal and visceral a book. As he traces their destinies, Stekel finds himself compelled to honor these young men, who like so many of their generation came from humble beginnings and reached within themselves to become ordinary people willing to do extraordinary things. I will not tip his hand, but as you read this book, be alert for Stekel's description of the military's determination to honor war dead, as well as his conversations with surviving family members.

When the news of the 2005 discovery broke, it was especially noteworthy in Hawaii, which is where WWII came ashore in the U.S. -- as well as being home to the forensic laboratory charged with identifying military remains from many times and places. Thanks to Stekel's research and determination, we now have a richer picture of these men's lives, their experiences in training, the equipment they and their comrades used, and sadly their deaths.

I haven't read this yet, since I bought it for my brother. However, I noticed that he took it off to bed for his nighttime reading...lol

First, as others have mentioned, the formatting and editing for the Kindle edition of this book is atrocious. Reading through error after error was annoying and distracting. Even if a book only costs .99, or in some cases, is even free, there is a certain standard that readers should be able to expect. What has book publishing come to if readers, in the name of a "good story" are expected to skim over and ignore frequent errors? If you are sensitive to this sort of thing, better move on to another title.

As for the actual novel, I didn't hate the story line. I found it at least compelling enough to read through to the end. Most romances are generally predictable. You know the girl is going to end up with the guy, and most of the time, you know which guy. It's the journey that makes you want to read anyway - because romance and love is fun. True to form, this romance is tremendously predictable - but the journey just doesn't pack enough punch to be worth the read. Characters are underdeveloped, the hero is too much of a minor character, and serious conflict is resolved through dialogue that is shallow, even silly.

The most frustrating aspect of this novel is the lack of consistency in narrative point of view. In mid-chapter, sometimes even in mid-paragraph, perspective jumps from the thoughts of one character, to the thoughts of another. For most of the novel, the perspective is third person limited omniscient, meaning we know only what is going on inside Anna, the main character's head. But occasionally, the author throws in a rogue paragraph that jumps into the head of another character supplying information that breaks point of view and is very distracting. As a seasoned reader, I found this to be incredibly amateurish. It's not impossible to write a novel that is completely omniscient, but it's difficult to execute well without your readers feeling like they are being tossed about.

Overall, while I feel like there were bones of a story that had potential, the execution just wasn't good enough to warrant my recommendation. I give it two stars because it stayed just interesting enough to make me read to the end, but not good enough for me to tell anyone else to read it.

Timbuctoo of the author Tahir Shah is a striking & intriguing reading that gradually takes us inexorably and inevitably to think about the cultural idea of freedom.
Timbuctoo is indeed a fast reading, grabbing the reader in its fast paced dialogue and the slow motion re-telling of traveling misfortunes.
Within few pages the predictability of the storytelling was surpassed by the image sequence that is being built, with the written tone and rhythmic flourishes from an Englishman from nineteenth century.
I did expected more details and more look & feel, tastes and scents from locales; but the story presented a variety of raw images of life from many cultural groups with different points of view upon territory, values, propriety, family and by doing so, Timbuctoo used cultural contrast as an art form.
Tahir Shah made a rare mix of literary scents from the 1001 nights with the voyages of Gulliver. He describes raw and violent human actions that are realistic
as Tarzan of Burroughs and yet his ending is very modern and some dialogues are extraordinary and worthy of a Wilde lot of literary gold meanings.
Structured like a novel or roman from Dumas that is vaguely familiar like an inverted Count of MonteCristo; the main character Adams, the accident traveler that survives many types of slavery and unwittingly reaches the city of Timbuctoo unwittingly reveals that strange and diverse societies may succumb to the same bad solutions to solve human affairs.  The story telling architecture repeats forms of control and constrain of others in different society systems encapsulating Adams as much as a prisioner in north subsaharian Africa as in Anglo-saxon islands.
The secondary money plot might not be very easy to classify as from a feuilleton in a newspaper sold in a caf circa 1856.  Although some counterpoint lines
of the narrative proposes extra undesired context detail, those do reassure the reader of the frame of mind of those that avidly listen to Adams tale.
Tahir Shah's Timbuctoo enriches with vivid images, takes out weight by avoiding emotional lengthy descriptions, sets the mind to see beyond discourse speech
and social lies, it is more than a travelogue of suffering slavery, it is a journey through perception of cultural behaviour, perhaps indicating
that there are many different forms of loosing freedom and that there are many different forms of fulfilling the hearts desire.
